Recent Changes to HIPAA Enforcement

Halfway through 2018, OCR had only agreed to three settlements with HIPAA-covered entities to resolve alleged HIPAA violations – a fraction of the level in the previous two years. It was starting to look like OCR was easing up on its enforcement of compliance with the HIPAA Rules; however, OCR announced many more settlements in the second half of the year and closed 2018 with 10 settlements and one civil monetary penalty – One more penalty than in 2017. 2018 ended up being a record year for HIPAA enforcement. The final total for fines and settlements was $28,683,400, which beat the previous record set in 2016 by 22%.

OCR’s enforcement activities continued at a high level in 2019, and OCR closed the year with 10 settlements and civil monetary penalties, totaling $12,274,000. In late 2019, OCR announced it was embarking on a new enforcement drive focused on compliance with the HIPAA Right of Access, which requires individuals to be provided with timely access to their medical records for only a reasonable, cost-based fee.

OCR settled two cases in 2019 under this initiative – both for $85,000 – and a further 11 settlements were announced in 2020 to resolve potential violations of the HIPAA Right of Access. In addition to noncompliance with the HIPAA Right of Access, in 2020, OCR imposed financial penalties for particularly egregious cases of noncompliance. The failure to conduct comprehensive risk analyses, poor risk management practices, lack of HIPAA policies and procedures, no business associate agreements, impermissible PHI disclosures, and a lack of safeguards all attracted HIPAA fines in 2020. 2020 saw more financial penalties imposed for violations of the HIPAA Rules than any other year, with the year closing with 19 settlements totaling $13,554,900.

There was a reduction in HIPAA enforcement actions in 2021, with 14 financial penalties announced to resolve HIPAA violations, the majority of which (12) were for violations of the HIPAA Right of Access. Aside from one financial penalty of $5,100,000 for Excellus Health Plan, the financial penalties were far lower in 2021 than in recent years, with penalties totaling $5,982,150 for the year. 2021 also saw an increase in the number of penalties for small healthcare providers.

The trend for smaller penalties continued in 2022, in part due to the nature of the HIPAA violations being enforced and also the new penalty structure OCR adopted (see the Penalty Structure for Violations of HIPAA Regulations in 2024 section below). OCR continued with its heavy focus on the enforcement of compliance with the HIPAA Right of Access, which typically involves a failure to provide one individual with a copy of their medical records, rather than widespread non-compliance with the HIPAA Rules. The average penalty amount in 2022 was $98,688, a quarter of the average penalty the previous year.

2022 saw more settlements and civil monetary penalties imposed (22) than in any other year to date, yet 2022 saw the lowest fine total since 2010, with $2,127,140 in financial penalties imposed. The second lowest of any full year since OCR was given the authority to enforce HIPAA compliance. Another trend that became clear in 2022 was OCR pursuing financial penalties against smaller healthcare organizations. 55% of all fines imposed in 2022 were on small medical practices.

There was a notable decline in penalties in 2023, with only 13 investigations resulting in settlements or civil monetary penalties, although there was a slight increase in fines, with $4,176,500 collected. Only 4 of the financial penalties resolved HIPAA Right of Access violations. One of the main reasons for fines was the failure to conduct a comprehensive, accurate, organization-wide risk analysis.

OCR launched a new HIPAA risk analysis enforcement initiative in 2023 and has provided considerable technical assistance to HIPAA-regulated entities on risk analyses. In its investigations of data breaches, OCR found that the lack of a security risk analysis and the failure to implement and adopt security risk management plans were significant deficiencies that contributed to security incidents and breaches. Under this initiative, OCR has imposed several financial penalties for risk analysis failures, and that enforcement initiative remains active in 2026. OCR has also indicated that it will be focusing its efforts on enforcing wider HIPAA Security Rule compliance.

Former OCR Director Melanie Fontes Rainer confirmed that 22 enforcement actions resulted in settlements or civil monetary penalties in 2024, making 2024 one of the most active years of HIPAA enforcement to date, although some of the cases closed in 2024 were not announced until 2025. OCR closed 2024 with 16 settlements/civil monetary penalties, and there were 21 settlements/civil monetary penalties announced by OCR in 2025.

In contrast to the past few years, there were relatively few enforcement actions in response to HIPAA Right of Access violations (5 penalties) in 2024, demonstrating that this compliance initiative has been effective at encouraging compliance with this Privacy Rule provision. Many of the enforcement actions in 2024 and 2025 resolved violations of the HIPAA Security Rule, with more than half resolving alleged violations of the risk analysis requirement of the HIPAA Security Rule.

In 2024, OCR collected more than $9.9 million in fines, with an average penalty of $579,003 in 2024. The biggest penalty was imposed on Montefiore Medical Center, with $4,750,000 paid to resolve multiple HIPAA Security Rule violations.

In 2025, OCR’s settlements and civil monetary penalties totaled $8,330,066, with an average penalty of $396,670 and a median penalty of $182,000. OCR has focused on one aspect of HIPAA Security Rule compliance – the risk analysis – which has allowed OCR to clear the backlog of investigations more quickly, albeit resulting in smaller, but more numerous penalties.

OCR has been petitioning Congress for further funding to support investigations of HIPAA violations and for Congress to increase the penalties for HIPAA violations. Former OCR Director Melanie Fontes Rainer confirmed that the HITECH and HIPAA audit program has been resurrected, and the third phase of HIPAA compliance audits is now underway, initially involving 50 audits of HIPAA-regulated entities. The audits are focused on HIPAA Security Rule compliance, especially the risk analysis and risk management requirements.

HIPAA Civil Monetary Penalty Overturned

In 2018, OCR imposed a civil monetary penalty of $4,348,000 on the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. OCR launched an investigation into three data breaches that collectively resulted in an impermissible disclosure of PHI of almost 35,000 individuals. The incidents occurred in 2012 and 2013 and involved the theft of an unencrypted laptop computer and two flash drives.

OCR determined MD Anderson had violated the HIPAA Rules by failing to encrypt the devices. In April 2019, MD Anderson appealed the fine, alleging that the HHS did not have the authority to impose the penalty and that it was excessive. In January 2021, the penalty was overturned, and OCR admitted it could not defend a fine of more than $450,000. The case was remanded for further proceedings, and the civil monetary penalties were vacated by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. The judge stated the civil monetary penalties were “arbitrary, capricious, and otherwise unlawful.”

The overturning of the HIPAA fine is thought to have forced OCR to change its approach to HIPAA enforcement, as the successful appeal may encourage other covered entities to appeal any proposed financial penalties for HIPAA violations. In 2022, financial penalties were imposed for a variety of reasons, but the majority were for HIPAA Right of Access violations, which appears to be safe ground. HIPAA enforcement in 2024 has encompassed a much wider range of HIPAA violations.

In an effort to improve efficiency, OCR restructured and created three new divisions to better utilize the skillsets of its staff. OCR has had a flat budget for years, but its workload has increased significantly, with a 69% increase in complaints between 2017 and 2022 and a 58% increase in data breaches between 2017 and 2021. The restructuring has made better use of OCR’s resources to improve efficiency, which has helped OCR address the current backlog of investigations and conduct more timely investigations, especially investigations of hacking incidents, as evidenced by the increase in settlements and civil monetary penalties in 2025.

Changes in OCR Leadership

In September 2021, 8 months into the Biden administration, Lisa J. Pino was appointed as the new OCR Director, taking over from acting OCR director Robinsue Frohboese, who headed the agency since the resignation of Roger Severino in January 2021. In contrast to past directors, Pino had cybersecurity and data breach experience, having served as a senior executive service official and senior counsel in the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Pino’s cybersecurity experience was expected to bring a change in how OCR conducts investigations of data breaches, especially in light of the HIPAA Safe Harbor Law. However, Piso left the role abruptly in July 2022, less than a year into her tenure, and Melanie Fontes Rainer was appointed OCR Director.

Melanie Fontes Rainer remained in the role until the administration change, when Anthony Archeval took the helm as Acting OCR Director until the appointment of Paula M. Stannard, who previously served as Senior Counselor and Advisor to former HHS Secretaries Tom Price and Alex Azar between 2017 and 2021 under the previous Trump administration, and Acting General Counsel and Deputy General Counsel for six years between 2003 and 2009 under the George W. Bush administration. She remains at the helm and looks set to implement major changes to the HIPAA Regulations – updates to both the HIPAA Privacy Rule and HIPAA Security Rule.

Penalty Structure for Violations of HIPAA Regulations in 2026

In 2019, there was a notable HIPAA change related to enforcement action. OCR issued a Notice of Enforcement Discretion after reinterpreting the requirements of the HITECH Act regarding penalties for non-compliance with the HIPAA Rules. The HITECH Act called for an increase in the penalties for non-compliance with the HIPAA Rules and, at the time, the HHS interpreted the language of the HITECH Act as requiring a cap of $1.5 million for HIPAA violations across all four penalty tiers. In 2019, the requirements of the HITECH Act were reassessed and interpreted differently. Rather than capping the penalties across all four tiers at the same amount, different maximum fines (adjusted for inflation) were set for each of the four tiers, as detailed in the table below.

Annual Penalty Limit Annual Penalty Limit Minimum Penalty per Violation Maximum Penalty per Violation Annual Penalty Cap Tier 1 Lack of Knowledge $141 $35,581 $35,581 Tier 2 Reasonable Cause $1,424 $71,162 $142,355 Tier 3 Willful Neglect $14,232 $71,162 $355,808 Tier 4 Willful neglect (not corrected within 30 days $71,162 $2,134,831 $2,134,831

This table reflects the penalty values published in the Federal Register on August 8, 2024, and the Enforcement Discretion Caps announced in April 2019. Since the change was addressed through a Notice of Enforcement Discretion, it is not legally binding but will remain in effect indefinitely.

The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) set the inflation multiplier for 2025 as 1.02598. The HHS has applied the multiplier for 2025, although due to the government shutdown for an extended period in 2025, OMB was unable to calculate an inflation multiplier for 2026. The HHS has confirmed that there will be no inflation increase in 2026 as a result. The multiplier set by OMB in 2027 will address any cost-of-living increases since the adjustment it set for 2025.

FTC Updates Health Breach Notification Rule

A great deal of health information is now collected, processed, and transmitted by entities not covered by HIPAA. That means that the health information is not classed as protected health information and is therefore not subject to the HIPAA Rules. Breaches of health information at HIPAA-regulated entities are subject to the requirements of the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, but if there is a breach at a non-HIPAA-regulated entity, it is subject to the Federal Trade Commission’s (FTC) Health Breach Notification Rule.

The FTC issued a final rule on April 26, 2024, updating the Health Breach Notification Rule with new and revised definitions to expand coverage to include health apps and other technologies not covered by HIPAA, including websites that collect health data that are not operated by HIPAA-regulated entities. The update also included new requirements for the content of consumer notifications and the requirement to notify the FTC of breaches of 500 or more records. The breach notification timeline is in line with HIPAA, with notifications required without undue delay and no later than 60 days from the date of discovery of a breach of security.

New HIPAA Regulations in 2021

While there were no changes to HIPAA regulations in 2021, new legislation was introduced related to the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules in terms of cybersecurity, patient access to healthcare data, and HIPAA enforcement.

2021 HIPAA Safe Harbor Law Updating the HITECH Act

On January 5, 2021, the HIPAA Safe Harbor Bill (HR 7898) was signed into law by President Trump and amended the HITECH Act. The purpose of the HIPAA Safe Harbor Bill was to encourage healthcare organizations to adopt “recognized security practices” to improve their defenses against cyberattacks. The HIPAA Safe Harbor Bill instructs the HHS to take into account the cybersecurity best practices that a HIPAA-regulated entity has adopted continuously for the 12 months preceding any data breach when considering HIPAA enforcement actions and calculating financial penalties related to security breaches and HIPAA Security Rule violations.

The name of the bill is a little misleading, as the HITECH Act amendment does not create a safe harbor where HIPAA-regulated entities avoid any audits or financial penalties for data breaches and/or HIPAA Security Rule violations. The bill requires the HHS to decrease the length and extent of any audits in response to those breaches if recognized security practices have been implemented, and financial penalties will be reduced, but not avoided entirely.

If a HIPAA-regulated entity can adequately demonstrate that recognized security practices have been implemented consistently for 12 months, it will be considered by OCR as a mitigating factor. Organizations that have adopted recognized security practices and have completed a HIPAA Security Risk Analysis, identified risks to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of electronic protected health information (ePHI) and have reduced them to a low and acceptable level, and have implemented technical safeguards to protect ePHI, will be treated more leniently by OCR. Financial penalties will not be increased for HIPAA-regulated entities that do not implement recognized security practices.

In addition to facing lower penalties and sanctions, HIPAA-regulated entities that adopt recognized security practices and are compliant with the requirements of the HIPAA Security Rule will be better protected against security incidents and data breaches.

21st Century Cures Act

The 21st Century Cures Act (Cures Act) of 2016 was introduced to encourage innovation in medical research, and one of the ways that this was achieved was to make it easier for patients to obtain their healthcare data and share that information with research institutions. The Cures Act called for the HHS to create a new Rule that would improve the flow of healthcare data between providers, patients, and developers of Health IT such as electronic health record (EHR) vendors.

The HHS’ Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) published its Interoperability and Information Blocking Final Rule in March 2020, and healthcare providers, developers of Certified Health IT, and health information networks or exchanges were given until November 2, 2020, comply with the information blocking provisions of the Final Rule, although the compliance date was then extended to April 5, 2021, due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) also published an interoperability rule in March 2020 that applies to Medicare- and Medicaid-participating short-term acute care hospitals, long-term care hospitals, rehabilitation hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, children’s hospitals, cancer hospitals, and critical access hospitals (CAHs). The compliance date for the CMS Rule was July 1, 2021, and CMS is now enforcing compliance.

Under the CMS Final Rule, CMS-regulated payers including Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations, Medicaid Fee-for-Service (FFS) programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP FFS programs, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers, must implement and maintain a secure, standards-based Application Programming Interface (API) to allow patients to access their claims and receive information through a third-party app of their choice, make provider directory information publicly available through a standards-based API, and send electronic patient event notifications of a patient’s admission, discharge, or transfer to another healthcare facility or another community provider or practitioner.

The final interoperability and information-blocking rules do not amend HIPAA or the HITECH Act, although they are related. The final rules promote patient access to ePHI and are intended to make access easier. It is possible that HIPAA policies and procedures could violate the ONC Final Rule if they include practices considered to constitute information blocking. Any entity that engages in information blocking can face financial penalties, which are capped at $1 million (adjusted annually for inflation).

New HIPAA Regulations FAQs Once a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking has been issued, is it guaranteed that there will be a change to the HIPAA Rules?

Once a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking has been issued, it is not guaranteed that there will be a change to the HIPAA Rules. For example, in 2014, the Department of Health & Human Services issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that would have required health plans to prove compliance with certain areas of the Administration Simplification standards via certification. The proposed Rule was withdrawn in 2017 due to concerns that it would place a significant burden on employers’ self-funded health plans.

Will there definitely be some new HIPAA regulations in 2027?

There are no guarantees that there will be any new HIPAA regulations in 2027, as while the proposed update to the HIPAA Security Rule has a target of July 2027 for a final rule, a decision has yet to be made by the HHS on whether it will proceed with a final rule. The July 2027 date is also not legally binding, and targets are often missed, so if a final rule is issued, it may well be delayed.

How much disruption might the new HIPAA regulations create?

Disruption caused by new HIPAA regulations depends on how many new HIPAA regulations are created by 2026 HIPAA final rules and how many of the changes are HIPAA amendments to existing standards rather than new requirements. It will be less disruptive to adapt existing policies and procedures to the new HIPAA amendments than it will be to accommodate completely new HIPAA regulations.

When a HIPAA Final Rule is published, will covered entities have to comply with it immediately?

When a HIPAA Final Rule is published, it is unlikely that covered entities will have to comply with it immediately. In most cases, covered entities have 90 or 180 days to comply with a rule change, depending on its complexity. When the original Privacy Rule Final Rule was published in 2002, covered entities were given a year to make systems, policies, and procedures HIPAA-compliant. Small health plans were given two years. If a HIPAA Final Rule is published, the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights will allow an appropriate period of time for covered entities (and business associates where applicable) to make the necessary adjustments – typically 180 days after the effective date.

Are HIPAA laws still in effect?

The HIPAA laws are still in effect unless a state has adopted regulations with more stringent privacy and security protections or greater individual rights. In some states, laws exist that have more stringent elements than HIPAA (for example, with regard to the privacy of AIDS patients), and in these states, the more stringent elements pre-empt the equivalent standards of HIPAA, but the remaining HIPAA laws are still in effect.

Can HIPAA be overturned?

HIPAA can be overturned by Congress, and, while there have been attempts in the past to repeal certain parts of the Act (for example, the requirement to develop a system of National Patient Identifiers), no part of HIPAA has been overturned to date. However, there have been numerous additions to HIPAA through the Rules added to the Administrative Simplification provisions and via the passage of the HITECH Act in 2009.

Will there be new HIPAA rules for text messaging and email in 2026?

There may new HIPAA rules for text messaging and email in 2026 due to the proposed “essential” HPH Cybersecurity Performance Goals setting a floor of safeguards to better protect organizations from cyberattacks. The safeguards include email system controls, multi-factor authentication, encryption, and workforce training.

Text messaging and email channels that do support the new HIPAA safeguards will not be considered suitable for HIPAA-compliant communications. For example, text messaging PHI via MS Teams covered by a Business Associate Agreement will be HIPAA compliant, but text messaging PHI via SMS will be a violation of HIPAA unless the recipient has specifically requested SMS communications and has been warned of the risks.

When was HIPAA last updated?

HIPAA was last updated in November 2026 when a final rule – HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens – was published. Prior to that, in April 2024, the HHS’ Office for Civil Rights published the HIPAA Final Rule to Support Reproductive Healthcare Privacy. The HIPAA Final Rule added a new section to the HIPAA Privacy Rule (§164.509) and introduced a new system of attestation for certain uses and disclosures of PHI. Most requirements have since been vacated by a federal judge. The requirement to revise HIPAA Notices of Privacy Practices remained and was extended until February 16, 2026, to align the revisions with those required by the Part 2 amendments.

Does HIPAA have to be signed yearly?

HIPAA does not have to be signed yearly, but Congress has to be kept informed of its effectiveness via several annual and semi-annual reports. Congress could – if it wished – repeal some or all of the Act, but so much of HIPAA is entwined with other state and federal privacy and security laws, that this is an unlikely option.

Do the changes to HIPAA in 2024 require policy revisions?

The changes to HIPAA in 2024 will require policy revisions when the changes impact a covered entity’s HIPAA-covered operations. For example, healthcare organizations that participate in a Part 2 program must revise their policies with regard to how SUD information is used and disclosed. In addition, the new HIPAA updates relating to the privacy of reproductive healthcare information will likely impact many healthcare organizations’ operations.

When were the most recent HIPAA changes to the HIPAA Privacy Rule?

The most recent HIPAA changes to the HIPAA Privacy Rule were finalized in November 2026 and modify the HIPAA Privacy Rule to strengthen the individual right of access to protected health information, facilitate care coordination, and reduce the regulatory burden on HIPAA covered entities. The changes finalized in the HIPAA Final Rule to Support Reproductive Healthcare Privacy have mostly been vacated and are not being enforced by OCR.

How will the proposed HIPAA changes of 2024 affect the Security Rule safeguards?

The proposed HIPAA changes in 2024 to support the Healthcare Sector Cybersecurity concept paper will affect the Security Rule safeguards, as the concept paper states there will be “new cybersecurity standards”. While these may affect some Administrative Safeguards (i.e., security management, contingency planning, and security awareness training), most of the new cybersecurity standards should appear as Technical Safeguards.

In the absence of new HIPAA regulations in 2024 to support Healthcare Sector Cybersecurity, the other proposed HIPAA changes in 2024 are unlikely to affect the Security Rule safeguards unless new implementation specifications are adopted to facilitate the transfer of PHI to personal health applications. Any other HIPAA changes to the Security Rule will more likely be in the Security Rule’s General Rules (45 CFR §164.306) rather than the Administrative, Physical, or Technical Safeguards.

What was the name of the last update to HIPAA?

The name of the last update to HIPAA is HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens, which was published in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026.  Prior to that, in April 2024, the HHS published a final rule called the “HIPAA Privacy Rule to Support Reproductive Health Care Privacy” (89 FR 32976).

Subsequent to these HIPAA updates, the most recent HIPAA update was published by HHS’ Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) in August 2024. This update relates to prior authorization processes and changes some Part 162 operating rules and exception processes. The short name of this update to HIPAA is “Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes” (89 FR 8758).

Where can I find the current HIPAA regulations?

To find the current HIPAA regulations, you can visit www.ecfr.gov and navigate to Title 45, Subtitle A, Subchapter C – “Administrative Data Standards and Related Requirements”. This Subchapter contains the current General Rule, Privacy Rule, Security Rule, and Breach Notification Rule, among other HIPAA regulations relating to data standards, enforcement procedures, and the imposition of fines.

It is important to be aware of other federal laws closely related to HIPAA (i.e., 42 CFR Part 2 and §1177 of the Social Security Act) and that some state laws pre-empt the HIPAA latest version or exempt HIPAA-covered entities. It is also important to be aware that the Combined Regulation Text published by the Department of Health and Human Services is not an up-to-date version of the current HIPAA regulations.

How often does HIPAA need to be updated?

There are no regulations that stipulate how often HIPAA needs to be updated. However, Parts of the Act are updated every few years to accommodate other acts of legislation (i.e., the NICS changes in 2016 were attributable to an amendment to the Brady Gun Law), to introduce new transaction codes for recently developed drugs and medical products, or to close loopholes in claims procedures. You can keep up to date with the latest HIPAA regulations by subscribing to HHS’ “OCR Privacy & Security Listserv”.

Will there be changes to the HIPAA laws regarding minors in 2026?

It is unlikely that there will be changes to the HIPAA laws regarding minors in 2026 based on how HHS’ Office for Civil Rights addressed the issue of “personal representatives” in the 2024 HIPAA changes to support the privacy of reproductive healthcare information. (“Nothing in this final rule is intended to alter any other use or disclosure permissions for personal representatives, nor does it interfere with the ability of states to define the nature of the relationship between a minor and a parent or guardian”).

Under HIPAA, minors are either “unemancipated” (i.e., subject to the control, authority, and supervision of their parents) or “emancipated” (i.e., living independently as an adult regardless of their age). As an unemancipated minor can be as old as 21 years in some jurisdictions and an emancipated minor as young as 14 years in others (subject to court approval), it would be difficult for HHS to change the HIPAA laws regarding minors in 2025 without creating further challenges with regard to minors’ personal representatives (i.e., parents, guardians, etc.) and providers’ good faith beliefs about what PHI should be disclosed to – or withheld from – minors’ personal representatives.

items.title: CVE-2026-114938: OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Vulnerable To Pre-Authentication RCE (Java4Shell)
items.summary: IntroductionOn November 17, 2026, security researchers from Calif.io publicly disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS v4.0: 9.2 Critical), a severe heap memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated (intrinsic) Base64 decoder on certain CPUs. The disclosure coincided with coordinated advisories from the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group and Oracle’s November 17, 2026 security patch release.Because Base64 decoding is foundational to network protocols, this runtime-level vulnerability can be reached in enterprise applications that pass attacker-controlled input to the affected decoder. Calif.io demonstrated pre-authentication Remote Code Execution (RCE) in default configurations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Additionally, post-authentication RCE was achieved in Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Netflix Spinnaker, as well as a client-side TLS exploit affecting Java clients connecting to a malicious server. Immediate patching for affected environments is strongly recommended, alongside other mitigation steps outlined in this advisory. Zscaler’s security team is actively analyzing this issue across both production and corporate environments. We will continue to update the Zscaler Trust post and this advisory as new information becomes available. RecommendationsOrganizations running Java workloads on x86-64 infrastructure should take the following actions:Apply vendor patches immediately: Upgrade OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM, and all downstream OpenJDK distributions to the patched builds released on or after November 17, 2026 (such as Oracle Java SE 17.0.21.1, 8u513, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1 security updates) and restart all running JVM processes and containers.Apply JVM flag workarounds where patching is delayed: If an immediate JDK upgrade is not feasible, defenders can completely disable the vulnerable assembly code path by passing either of the following flags at JVM startup (e.g., via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS):-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics (Recommended): Disables hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding intrinsics across all architectures, falling back to safe Java bytecode execution.-XX:UseAVX=2 (x86-64 hosts only): Restricts HotSpot to AVX2 instructions, preventing the use of AVX-512 VBMI instructions. Warning: Use this flag only on x86-64 machines; OpenJDK on ARM64 does not recognize this flag and will fail to start.After adjusting startup command lines and parameters, restart all running JVM processes and containers.Check Host CPUs for AVX-512 VBMI Exposure: Because CVE-2026-114938 is hardware-dependent, administrators can determine if the CPU of a Linux system is capable of executing the vulnerable Base64 decoder by inspecting the /proc/cpuinfo file and determining if all four of the following flags are present: avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2. If a system is not susceptible, the JVM patches should still be applied in accordance with local policy and best practices.Eliminate public exposure: Place internet-facing Java applications (such as Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory, and PingFederate) behind Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).Enable reverse-proxy request buffering (Defense-in-Depth): Many remote heap grooming techniques rely on partial HTTP requests to prepare the heap for successful exploitation. Enabling full HTTP request-body buffering at the reverse proxy (e.g., Nginx proxy_request_buffering on;) disrupts multi-connection timing alignment—though note this is not a complete mitigation for single-request chains (such as Elasticsearch) or upgraded WebSocket tunnels. Affected JDK Distributions And VersionsCVE-2026-114938 affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer, as well as specific performance/patch builds across Oracle Java SE and downstream OpenJDK distributions as shown in the table below:Vendor / CategoryAffected Products & VersionsRemediation / PatchOpenJDK (Upstream)8.5.0 – 8.5.11Apply OpenJDK 2026-11-17 advisory patches, or if patching is delayed, use -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround.Oracle Java SE / Oracle GraalVM8.4.0 – 8.4.26Upgrade to the applicable Oracle November 17, 2026 patch (e.g., Java SE 17.0.21.1).Downstream OpenJDK DistributionsAmazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDKUpgrade to a build that fixes CVE-2026-114938, or if patching is delayed, apply -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround.Table 1: Affected JDK distributions and versions.Hardware prerequisitesThe vulnerable assembly routine is only emitted by the HotSpot C2 JIT compiler on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI (avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, bmi2):Vulnerable Intel server CPUs: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, and Granite RapidsVulnerable AMD server and desktop CPUs: AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer (e.g., EPYC Genoa / Bergamo / Turin, Ryzen 7000/9000 series)Not affected: ARM64 processors (e.g., AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon, Ampere Altra) and older x86-64 CPUs lacking AVX-512 VBMI. Technical AnalysisHow it worksWhile Java is traditionally regarded as a memory-safe language that abstracts raw pointer arithmetic away from developers, the OpenJDK HotSpot Virtual Machine itself relies heavily on C, C++, and hand-rolled assembly intrinsics to maximize throughput on modern hardware. Specifically, OpenJDK’s C2 Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler includes an optimized x86-64 Base64 decoding routine leveraging AVX-512 VBMI vector instructions. Due to an arithmetic underflow when calculating the store mask for improperly padded Base64 tails, malformed Base64 input can be used to trigger a 62-byte heap out-of-bounds write.Base64 decoding sits at the foundation of many network protocols including HTTP authentication, cookies, authorization tokens, TLS certificate parsing, REST API payloads, and file uploads. Thus, the attack surface for this vulnerability is significant. The figure below shows how malformed input can lead to heap corruption.Figure 1: CVE-2026-114938: Java4Shell Exploit Workflow ConclusionCVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) demonstrates that even memory-safe managed runtimes like Java are susceptible to classic memory corruption when low-level assembly intrinsics miscalculate bounds. Organizations running affected Java builds on x86-64 processors with the required instruction support should patch immediately . Where immediate patching is not possible, restart affected JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to temporarily disable the vulnerable code path. Zscaler CoverageZscaler has deployed the following protections for CVE-2026-114938:Zscaler DeceptionZscaler Deception customers can deploy Private Threat Intelligence decoys for the following applications to detect Java4Shell exploitation attempts and generate high-fidelity alerts:Apache SolrJenkinsAtlassian ConfluenceAtlassian JiraElasticsearchCustomers can configure an orchestration rule to add any IP addresses interacting with these decoys to a firewall block list. How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table outlines typical attack stages for CVE-2026-114938 and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler:Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify and prioritize vulnerable Java deployments with Zscaler Exposure Management; eliminate externally exposed internal Java applications by placing them behind Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).Prevent compromiseInspect inbound and outbound traffic with ZPA and Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to detect and block malformed Base64 padding tails, protect Java clients against the client-side TLS exploit vector by routing egress traffic through ZIA with full SSL/TLS inspection.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app and app-to-app microsegmentation for crown-jewel workloads, deploy Zscaler Deception decoys to detect lateral movement.Use Zscaler Microsegmentation to restrict workload-to-workload traffic and limit lateral movement if a Java workload is compromised.Prevent data lossInspect outbound responses and egress traffic across all channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP) to detect and block JavaBleed heap memory leaks containing private keys, credentials, or PII. Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Network-level indicatorsJIT warm-up floods: High volumes of rapid, repetitive requests containing valid Base64 fields targeting endpoints that invoke java.util.Base64.Decoder.Connection parking (remote heap grooming): Multiple concurrent TCP/HTTP connections from the same source IP delivering partial HTTP request bodies, pausing awaiting TCP ACK, and releasing the final bytes simultaneously.Malformed Base64 tail triggers: Base64 strings whose length is a multiple of 64 bytes (64 or 128 characters) immediately followed by an invalid padded tail (=, ==, X=, X==, XY=, ===), such as AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= (64 bytes + =) or 128 × "A" + "=".JavaBleed response anomalies: Abnormally large HTTP responses returned immediately after a spike in IllegalArgumentException errors.Host-level indicatorsSpikes in java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: High rates of IllegalArgumentException: Illegal base64 character or invalid padding exceptions in application logs.JVM crash logs (hs_err_pid*.log): Repeated HotSpot SIGSEGV crashes in G1 GC routines or StubRoutines::base64_decodeBlock.Suspicious JVM child processes: Java process spawning unexpected OS shells or reconnaissance commands.

How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table outlines typical attack stages for CVE-2026-114938 and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler:Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify and prioritize vulnerable Java deployments with Zscaler Exposure Management; eliminate externally exposed internal Java applications by placing them behind Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).Prevent compromiseInspect inbound and outbound traffic with ZPA and Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to detect and block malformed Base64 padding tails, protect Java clients against the client-side TLS exploit vector by routing egress traffic through ZIA with full SSL/TLS inspection.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app and app-to-app microsegmentation for crown-jewel workloads, deploy Zscaler Deception decoys to detect lateral movement.Use Zscaler Microsegmentation to restrict workload-to-workload traffic and limit lateral movement if a Java workload is compromised.Prevent data lossInspect outbound responses and egress traffic across all channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP) to detect and block JavaBleed heap memory leaks containing private keys, credentials, or PII.  Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Network-level indicatorsJIT warm-up floods: High volumes of rapid, repetitive requests containing valid Base64 fields targeting endpoints that invoke java.util.Base64.Decoder.Connection parking (remote heap grooming): Multiple concurrent TCP/HTTP connections from the same source IP delivering partial HTTP request bodies, pausing awaiting TCP ACK, and releasing the final bytes simultaneously.Malformed Base64 tail triggers: Base64 strings whose length is a multiple of 64 bytes (64 or 128 characters) immediately followed by an invalid padded tail (=, ==, X=, X==, XY=, ===), such as AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= (64 bytes + =) or 128 × "A" + "=".JavaBleed response anomalies: Abnormally large HTTP responses returned immediately after a spike in IllegalArgumentException errors.Host-level indicatorsSpikes in java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: High rates of IllegalArgumentException: Illegal base64 character or invalid padding exceptions in application logs.JVM crash logs (hs_err_pid*.log): Repeated HotSpot SIGSEGV crashes in G1 GC routines or StubRoutines::base64_decodeBlock.Suspicious JVM child processes: Java process spawning unexpected OS shells or reconnaissance commands.

items.title: Treat Your Honeypot Analysis Like Code: Git, Pull Requests and a Human Gate for AI [Guest Diary], (Wed, Nov 18th)
items.summary: [This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] Introduction When conducting analysis of honeypot activity, it's easy for it to start as a pile of terminal output. The process is manual; screenshots of the terminal, plus a text file that gets edited in a common word processing application until it is "done". There is no say whether a certain number came from a certain query, what changed between drafts, or who decided to drop a caveat. While hosting my own honeypot sensor, I wrote up three attacks: An SSH brute force that logged in as mysql/mysql [ 1 ] A bot looking for Telegram Desktop sessions and SMS modems [ 2 ] A month of RedTail exploits against PHP plus one oversized multipart POST that matches the shape of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) [ 3 ]. Instead of a document folder though, I kept every report in a public git repository [ 4 ] and changed it only through pull requests. Supporting me in my analysis was an AI coding agent (Claude Code), which also drafted reports as a separate GitHub machine account. I wanted to give my Claude Code sessions a tangible identity in the code submission and review process, where a dedicated GitHub account could propose changes but never approve or merge them. Even though I drove every part of the analysis process, the code review of each pull request marked a deliberate step in my workflow which acted as both a gate and a spot-check of the content I was producing. This diary describes that setup, what the git history shows about how well it worked, and what I would change. Why Do It The question this post answers are: can version control and a mandatory human review make AI-drafted security analysis trustworthy enough to publish? It matters for three reasons: Reproducibility . An indicator list or a timeline is only as good as the query behind it. If the query and its output are stored next to the claim, anyone can check it. Public safety . Honeypot reports contain things that must not be published: the sensor's own address, its hostname, its cloud account, and sometimes attacker material such as private keys. Once something reaches a public git history, deleting the file does not remove it [ 4 , SECURITY.md]. AI accountability . Language models are fluent and are confident; but fluency and confidence don't mean accuracy. If an AI is part of the workflow, there needs to be a record of what it wrote, what a human changed, and who approved it. The Setup The repository has one folder per attack. Each folder holds the summary, every piece of evidence it cites, and a hash list: Every exhibit in a report's appendix shows the exact jq query that produced it, for example: Before anything leaves the sensor, output is passed through a filter that replaces the sensor's address with , and then hashed. Anyone who clones the repository can confirm the evidence has not changed since it was committed: The workflow around those files is shown in Figure 1. The important pieces are: A separate identity for the AI. Pull requests from the machine account are written by Claude Code sessions. It is a machine account I operate, and the README says so publicly [ 4 ]. The AI can write but not merge. A GitHub ruleset on main requires a pull request with one approval, blocks force-pushes and branch deletion and has no bypass actors. The AI account has written access, but GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so it can never get a change into main alone. A public-safety checklist on every PR. The pull request template asks the author to confirm that they read the full diff, that the secret scan is clean, that every IP and account is a placeholder (attacker indicators excepted), that there are no hostnames or local paths, and that attachments were checked by hand. The AI fills this in and I check it. A secret scanner before every commit. A pre-commit hook runs gitleaks locally. Options to Close Gaps Comparing the ruleset with my own design notes [4, homelab/change-control.md] showed where the live settings fall short: Fortunately, none of these needs’ new tools. These are repository settings and habits, which is the point. The controls that are deployed are the ones enforced by the server (GitHub), not ones written into a file the AI could edit on its own branch. Who Benefits Students and new analysts get a structure that forces each claim to point at evidence, and a history that shows a reviewer how their analysis improved. This works as a solo project, but the benefits grow exponentially with multiple analysts and reviewers. Honeypot operators and DShield contributors can publish findings with less risk of leaking their sensor's identity, because the scrubbing and checklist happen before a merge, not after. Teams adopting AI assistants get a pattern they can copy: a separate identity for the AI, server-side merge controls, and a checklist that the AI must fill in honestly. The record shows exactly where the AI's work ended and a human's began. Readers of the reports can verify them. Every indicator traces to a query, and every query's output has a hash. Conclusion Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code. That said though, treating something like honeypot/log analysis like code gave me reproducible evidence, a reviewable history, and a safe way to use an AI drafter: it proposed, I reviewed, and only I could merge. The history also kept me honest about the parts that did not work. Those gaps are visible because the work was in git, and each has a simple fix in the repository settings. References [1] Honeypot Attack Summary: SSH Brute Force from 77.239.124.204. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-18-ssh-brute-force-mysql-default-creds [2] Honeypot Attack Summary: Telegram Session and SMS Modem Reconnaissance Bot. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-19-telegram-sms-recon-bot [3] Honeypot Attack Summary: PHP Vulnerability Hunt, RedTail and a PHP2Shell-Pattern Request. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-03-php-vulnerability-hunt [4] kevtruo/security repository (README, SECURITY.md, pull request template,homelab/change-control.md). https://github.com/kevtruo/security [5] GitHub Docs, "About rulesets." https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets [6] GitHub Docs, "About push protection." https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/introduction/about-push-protection [7] gitleaks. https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks [8] Claude Code GitHub Actions documentation. https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/github-action [9] https://www.sans.edu/cyber-security-programs/bachelors-degree/ ----------- Guy Bruneau IPSS Inc. [This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Introduction
When conducting analysis of honeypot activity, it's easy for it to start as a pile of terminal output. The process is manual; screenshots of the terminal, plus a text file that gets edited in a common word processing application until it is "done". There is no say whether a certain number came from a certain query, what changed between drafts, or who decided to drop a caveat.


While hosting my own honeypot sensor, I wrote up three attacks:

  • An SSH brute force that logged in as mysql/mysql [1]
  • A bot looking for Telegram Desktop sessions and SMS modems [2]
  • A month of RedTail exploits against PHP plus one oversized multipart POST that matches the shape of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) [3].

Instead of a document folder though, I kept every report in a public git repository [4] and changed it only through pull requests. Supporting me in my analysis was an AI coding agent (Claude Code), which also drafted reports as a separate GitHub machine account. I wanted to give my Claude Code sessions a tangible identity in the code submission and review process, where a dedicated GitHub account could propose changes but never approve or merge them. 

Even though I drove every part of the analysis process, the code review of each pull request marked a deliberate step in my workflow which acted as both a gate and a spot-check of the content I was producing.

This diary describes that setup, what the git history shows about how well it worked, and what I would change.

Why Do It

The question this post answers are: can version control and a mandatory human review make AI-drafted security analysis trustworthy enough to publish?

It matters for three reasons:

  • Reproducibility. An indicator list or a timeline is only as good as the query behind it. If the query and its output are stored next to the claim, anyone can check it.
  • Public safety. Honeypot reports contain things that must not be published: the sensor's own address, its hostname, its cloud account, and sometimes attacker material such as private keys. Once something reaches a public git history, deleting the file does not remove it [4, SECURITY.md].
  • AI accountability. Language models are fluent and are confident; but fluency and confidence don't mean accuracy. If an AI is part of the workflow, there needs to be a record of what it wrote, what a human changed, and who approved it.

The Setup

The repository has one folder per attack. Each folder holds the summary, every piece of evidence it cites, and a hash list:

Every exhibit in a report's appendix shows the exact jq query that produced it, for example:

Before anything leaves the sensor, output is passed through a filter that replaces the sensor's address with , and then hashed. Anyone who clones the repository can confirm the evidence has not changed since it was committed:

The workflow around those files is shown in Figure 1.

The important pieces are:

  • A separate identity for the AI. Pull requests from the machine account are written by Claude Code sessions. It is a machine account I operate, and the README says so publicly [4].
  • The AI can write but not merge. A GitHub ruleset on main requires a pull request with one approval, blocks force-pushes and branch deletion and has no bypass actors. The AI account has written access, but GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so it can never get a change into main alone.
  • A public-safety checklist on every PR. The pull request template asks the author to confirm that they read the full diff, that the secret scan is clean, that every IP and account is a placeholder (attacker indicators excepted), that there are no hostnames or local paths, and that attachments were checked by hand. The AI fills this in and I check it.
  • A secret scanner before every commit. A pre-commit hook runs gitleaks locally.

Options to Close Gaps

Comparing the ruleset with my own design notes [4, homelab/change-control.md] showed where the live settings fall short:

Fortunately, none of these needs’ new tools. These are repository settings and habits, which is the point. The controls that are deployed are the ones enforced by the server (GitHub), not ones written into a file the AI could edit on its own branch.

Who Benefits

  • Students and new analysts get a structure that forces each claim to point at evidence, and a history that shows a reviewer how their analysis improved. This works as a solo project, but the benefits grow exponentially with multiple analysts and reviewers.
  • Honeypot operators and DShield contributors can publish findings with less risk of leaking their sensor's identity, because the scrubbing and checklist happen before a merge, not after.
  • Teams adopting AI assistants get a pattern they can copy: a separate identity for the AI, server-side merge controls, and a checklist that the AI must fill in honestly. The record shows exactly where the AI's work ended and a human's began.
  • Readers of the reports can verify them. Every indicator traces to a query, and every query's output has a hash.

Conclusion

Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code. That said though, treating something like honeypot/log analysis like code gave me reproducible evidence, a reviewable history, and a safe way to use an AI drafter: it proposed, I reviewed, and only I could merge. The history also kept me honest about the parts that did not work. Those gaps are visible because the work was in git, and each has a simple fix in the repository settings.

References

[1] Honeypot Attack Summary: SSH Brute Force from 77.239.124.204. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-18-ssh-brute-force-mysql-default-creds
[2] Honeypot Attack Summary: Telegram Session and SMS Modem Reconnaissance Bot. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-19-telegram-sms-recon-bot
[3] Honeypot Attack Summary: PHP Vulnerability Hunt, RedTail and a PHP2Shell-Pattern Request. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-03-php-vulnerability-hunt
[4] kevtruo/security repository (README, SECURITY.md, pull request template,homelab/change-control.md). https://github.com/kevtruo/security
[5] GitHub Docs, "About rulesets." https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets
[6] GitHub Docs, "About push protection." https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/introduction/about-push-protection
[7] gitleaks. https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
[8] Claude Code GitHub Actions documentation. https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/github-action

items.title: Attackers Exploit Optimizely Flaw To Inject Malicious JavaScript
items.summary: IntroductionOn November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow. Optimizely is a platform used to create, manage, test, and personalize digital content and websites. The flaw allowed the attacker to edit the Project JavaScript (projectJS) field. Customers use this field to add custom code that runs on pages that load the Optimizely snippet. By abusing this mechanism, the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The code was then delivered to visitors’ browsers through the Optimizely snippets, including snippets served from Optimizely’s content delivery network (CDN).The attack highlights the continued risk posed by third-party script dependencies and software supply chain compromises, particularly when websites rely on trusted third-party platforms to deliver JavaScript that runs in visitors’ browsers.Optimizely reported that it blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code from affected projects, ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts, and notified impacted customers.The malicious payload was designed to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skim payment card details, steal cookies, capture page screenshots, and deliver iOS exploits to iPhones and iPads. Organizations using Optimizely, or similar third-party JavaScript platforms, should treat this incident as a reminder to review third-party script governance, monitoring, and browser-side security controls. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz identified more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script. These findings suggest a broader impact across organizations and industry verticals than previously reported. The affected domains span industries including the following:Airlines and TravelAutomotiveBanking and FinanceE-commerceInsuranceNews and MediaProperty and Real EstateRetail and FashionSmart HomeSportsTechnology and SaaSTelecommunications RecommendationsFor end users who visited affected sitesMonitor bank and credit card statements for suspicious activity.Review cryptocurrency transactions made on or around November 16, 2026.Be cautious of unexpected account activity on sites visited during the incident.Update iOS and iPadOS devices to the latest available security version.Change passwords for accounts used on potentially affected websites, especially if the same credentials are reused elsewhere.For organizations using OptimizelyReview Optimizely project configurationAudit all Project JavaScript fields for unauthorized or unexpected code.Review recent changes, user activity, account creation events, and administrative access.Confirm whether any project snippets were modified during the exposure window.Verify that production pages load only approved versions of Optimizely snippets.Rotate and reset accessReset credentials for affected Optimizely administrative users.Rotate API tokens, session tokens, and integration keys associated with Optimizely.Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users with access to experimentation or web personalization platforms.Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) in enforcement mode where possibleRestrict script execution to approved domains.Limit where pages can send requests and load images and frames using connect-src, img-src, frame-src, and related CSP directives.Use CSP reporting to identify unexpected browser-side activity.Reduce third-party JavaScript riskMaintain an inventory of third-party scripts loaded across websites.Review whether each third-party script is still required.Apply least-privilege principles to third-party tags and tag management platforms.Monitor third-party script changes and unexpected behavior. How It WorksOptimizely Web Experimentation allows site owners to run A/B tests, personalization logic, and other front-end experiments by loading JavaScript on customer websites. The Project JavaScript field is designed to let customers add custom JavaScript that executes on any page that loads the Optimizely snippet.Public reporting indicates that the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into the Project JavaScript field of affected customer projects. The injected code was then delivered through legitimate Optimizely snippets. As a result, when visitors loaded a page with a modified snippet, the injected JavaScript could run in their browsers.Scope of script activity: The observed JavaScript activity is primarily limited to the browser context of the website where the scripts are loaded. The wallet replacement, clipboard manipulation, form monitoring, card-skimming, screen capture, and network-hooking behaviors operate inside the current page, its accessible DOM, same-origin frames, page-initiated requests, and JavaScript-accessible cookies or browser APIs. By design, this JavaScript cannot directly inspect other browser tabs, unrelated websites, other sites’ cookies, local files, or global browser activity. The main exception is the iOS/iPadOS exploit-delivery branch: if one of the delivered exploit chains succeeds, the resulting impact could potentially exceed normal web-page sandbox restrictions.Attack chainThe figure below shows how malicious JavaScript reached website visitors through Optimizely snippets.Figure 1: Attack chain showing how a threat actor injected malicious JavaScript into Optimizely customer projects.Initial access and injectionAs stated above, the attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation account signup flow. This flaw allowed unauthorized write access to the Project JavaScript field for multiple customer projects. Modified snippets were served through existing delivery paths, including Optimizely’s CDN (including cdn.optimizely.com) and, in some cases, customer domains. This made the attack more effective because many affected websites already trusted and allowed Optimizely scripts.Malicious JavaScript payloadIn most affected snippets, the injected code acted as a loader that fetched a second-stage JavaScript payload named track.js from attacker-controlled infrastructure such as 1688360[.]cc. The JavaScript payload provided the main malicious functionality, and ran in the visitor’s browser within the context of the affected website.The following flowchart shows what track.js does after it runs in a visitor’s browser. Figure 2: Clipboard hijacking, card skimming, cookie theft, screen capturing, and attempted exploit delivery on iOS and iPadOS.Cryptocurrency address replacement The script monitors page content, clipboard operations, and network-transmitted data for cryptocurrency wallet addresses. Targeted cryptocurrencies include Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana, Litecoin, Toncoin, Bitcoin Cash, and Dogecoin. When the script detects a valid wallet address, the script attempts to replace it with an attacker-controlled wallet address. Cookie theft and screen capture Cookie theft and screen capture happens only when a valid crypto wallet address is replaced and the element is visible. In that case, the JavaScript payload script loaded the legitimate html2canvas.min.js to capture a screenshot of the page, along with the page URL, cookies, original wallet address, and other metadata. This data is sent to the attacker endpoint https://1688360[.]cc/hit.php, likely so the operator can validate successful replacement activity and capture the victim’s session context. The JavaScript payload could collect browser cookies from the affected website, with some exceptions such as if the HttpOnly flag was set. This could cause users to unknowingly send cryptocurrency to the attacker instead of the intended recipient.Payment card skimmingLater versions of the payload added payment card skimming functionality. The script monitors input and textarea elements, keyboard events, form submissions, and web requests for payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV values on the compromised website. Captured card data was to an attacker-controlled endpoint (1688360[.]cc/card.php). Note the skimmer could not read payment details entered inside secure cross-origin payment iframes, such as hosted payment fields from providers like Stripe or Adyen.Attempted iOS exploit delivery For visitors using iPhones or iPads, the malware reportedly attempted to load the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits. The payload used device and browser checks to decide whether to attempt iOS-specific exploitation. When the payload identified a visitor’s device as an iPhone or iPad, it added two script elements to the page to load external JavaScript files. Indicators of these pages are the elements data-channel-code, data-chain-url, and data-cfasync attributes.The script injected a hidden iframe in some cases (hxxps://eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu/JIUJIU888/weifile[.]html) on devices it identified as running iOS 18.6 or earlier. The iframe is positioned off-screen with zero width and height, suggesting it is not intended to be visible to the user. iOS exploit delivery componentstrack.js is the browser-side payload. It checks for iOS or iPadOS and loads additional components when it detects either operating system.boot.js is the main iOS loader. It uses Safari and iOS version information to select the next delivery path.weifile.html provides a separate delivery path for selected iOS and iPadOS versions. It loads index.js.index.js initializes an obfuscated loader, decodes embedded modules, reports device and domain metadata, and may fetch additional modules (if required). The following table summarizes the two modules embedded in index.js.Embedded Module IdentifierDescription57620206d62079baad0e57e6d9ec93120c0f5247Utility/runtime helper module providing encoding, binary parsing, numeric conversion, URL normalization, and typed-array/DataView helpers.14669ca3b1519ba2a8f40be287f646d4d7593eb0Browser environment profiling and anti-analysis module that checks runtime capabilities, storage behavior, WebRTC, MathML rendering, WebAssembly behavior, and automation indicators such as navigator.webdriver.Table 1: Functions of the two modules embedded in index.js. ConclusionThe Optimizely incident highlights how attackers can compromise trusted third-party JavaScript supply chains to reach users across many websites at once. By abusing a legitimate experimentation feature, the attacker delivered injected JavaScript through snippets that affected websites already trusted. Note the malicious JavaScript code can run in visitors’ browsers without any obvious change to the page. The card-skimming and wallet-replacement behavior should be understood as page-context activity, not browser-wide monitoring. These scripts act within the compromised site where they are loaded. Broader impact would depend on successful exploitation by the iOS/WebKit exploit chain. Zscaler CoverageThe Zscaler ThreatLabz team has deployed protections for the indicators of compromise associated with this campaign.Zscaler Advanced Threat ProtectionHTML.Malurl.OPZHTML.Phish.Gen.LVHTML.Malurl.Gentp.LZHTML.Phish.Gen.Rc.A.ENHTML.Malurl.Gen.LZJS.PWS.Optimizely How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table shows Zscaler’s recommended mitigations by attack stage.Attack StageRecommended MitigationPrevent compromiseEnable SSL/TLS inspection for all traffic, including trusted sources.Use Advanced Threat Protection to detect malicious scripts. Configure policies to block Newly Registered and Observed Domains.Route server egress through Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to detect and block post-compromise activity.Use Advanced Cloud Firewall to extend controls across all ports/protocols.Use Zscaler Zero Trust Browser to isolate high-risk browsing sessions and reduce endpoint exposure to malicious web content.Prevent lateral threat movementUse Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) to enforce least-privilege user-to-application segmentation.Use Zscaler Deception to detect attacker movement after initial compromise. Monitor for suspicious access to internal applications following web application crashes or abnormal behavior.Detect post-exploitation activityUse Zscaler Managed Detection & Response (MDR) and Threat Hunting to investigate suspicious process behavior, command execution, unusual outbound connections, container runtime anomalies, and web application worker crashes.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP).Monitor for unusual uploads, archive transfers, credential exposure, or data movement following suspected exploitation. Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Domains and URLsIOCTypeDetails1688360[.]ccDomainMain domain associated with the threat campaign. Also used for fingerprinting, reporting, and screenshot submission by track.js. Includes the following URLs:1688360[.]cc/hit.php1688360[.]cc/html2canvas.min.js1688360[.]cc/track.js1688360[.]cc/card.phpeil786npto9u5bq[.]icuDomainHosts another iOS boot.js script and the weifile.html iframe path. items.summary_html: IntroductionOn November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow. Optimizely is a platform used to create, manage, test, and personalize digital content and websites. The flaw allowed the attacker to edit the Project JavaScript (projectJS) field. Customers use this field to add custom code that runs on pages that load the Optimizely snippet. By abusing this mechanism, the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The code was then delivered to visitors’ browsers through the Optimizely snippets, including snippets served from Optimizely’s content delivery network (CDN).The attack highlights the continued risk posed by third-party script dependencies and software supply chain compromises, particularly when websites rely on trusted third-party platforms to deliver JavaScript that runs in visitors’ browsers.Optimizely reported that it blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code from affected projects, ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts, and notified impacted customers.The malicious payload was designed to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skim payment card details, steal cookies, capture page screenshots, and deliver iOS exploits to iPhones and iPads. Organizations using Optimizely, or similar third-party JavaScript platforms, should treat this incident as a reminder to review third-party script governance, monitoring, and browser-side security controls. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz identified more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script. These findings suggest a broader impact across organizations and industry verticals than previously reported. The affected domains span industries including the following:Airlines and TravelAutomotiveBanking and FinanceE-commerceInsuranceNews and MediaProperty and Real EstateRetail and FashionSmart HomeSportsTechnology and SaaSTelecommunications RecommendationsFor end users who visited affected sitesMonitor bank and credit card statements for suspicious activity.Review cryptocurrency transactions made on or around November 16, 2026.Be cautious of unexpected account activity on sites visited during the incident.Update iOS and iPadOS devices to the latest available security version.Change passwords for accounts used on potentially affected websites, especially if the same credentials are reused elsewhere.For organizations using OptimizelyReview Optimizely project configurationAudit all Project JavaScript fields for unauthorized or unexpected code.Review recent changes, user activity, account creation events, and administrative access.Confirm whether any project snippets were modified during the exposure window.Verify that production pages load only approved versions of Optimizely snippets.Rotate and reset accessReset credentials for affected Optimizely administrative users.Rotate API tokens, session tokens, and integration keys associated with Optimizely.Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users with access to experimentation or web personalization platforms.Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) in enforcement mode where possibleRestrict script execution to approved domains.Limit where pages can send requests and load images and frames using connect-src, img-src, frame-src, and related CSP directives.Use CSP reporting to identify unexpected browser-side activity.Reduce third-party JavaScript riskMaintain an inventory of third-party scripts loaded across websites.Review whether each third-party script is still required.Apply least-privilege principles to third-party tags and tag management platforms.Monitor third-party script changes and unexpected behavior. How It WorksOptimizely Web Experimentation allows site owners to run A/B tests, personalization logic, and other front-end experiments by loading JavaScript on customer websites. The Project JavaScript field is designed to let customers add custom JavaScript that executes on any page that loads the Optimizely snippet.Public reporting indicates that the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into the Project JavaScript field of affected customer projects. The injected code was then delivered through legitimate Optimizely snippets. As a result, when visitors loaded a page with a modified snippet, the injected JavaScript could run in their browsers.Scope of script activity: The observed JavaScript activity is primarily limited to the browser context of the website where the scripts are loaded. The wallet replacement, clipboard manipulation, form monitoring, card-skimming, screen capture, and network-hooking behaviors operate inside the current page, its accessible DOM, same-origin frames, page-initiated requests, and JavaScript-accessible cookies or browser APIs. By design, this JavaScript cannot directly inspect other browser tabs, unrelated websites, other sites’ cookies, local files, or global browser activity. The main exception is the iOS/iPadOS exploit-delivery branch: if one of the delivered exploit chains succeeds, the resulting impact could potentially exceed normal web-page sandbox restrictions.Attack chainThe figure below shows how malicious JavaScript reached website visitors through Optimizely snippets.Figure 1: Attack chain showing how a threat actor injected malicious JavaScript into Optimizely customer projects.Initial access and injectionAs stated above, the attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation account signup flow. This flaw allowed unauthorized write access to the Project JavaScript field for multiple customer projects. Modified snippets were served through existing delivery paths, including Optimizely’s CDN (including cdn.optimizely.com) and, in some cases, customer domains. This made the attack more effective because many affected websites already trusted and allowed Optimizely scripts.Malicious JavaScript payloadIn most affected snippets, the injected code acted as a loader that fetched a second-stage JavaScript payload named track.js from attacker-controlled infrastructure such as 1688360[.]cc. The JavaScript payload provided the main malicious functionality, and ran in the visitor’s browser within the context of the affected website.The following flowchart shows what track.js does after it runs in a visitor’s browser. Figure 2: Clipboard hijacking, card skimming, cookie theft, screen capturing, and attempted exploit delivery on iOS and iPadOS.Cryptocurrency address replacement The script monitors page content, clipboard operations, and network-transmitted data for cryptocurrency wallet addresses. Targeted cryptocurrencies include Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana, Litecoin, Toncoin, Bitcoin Cash, and Dogecoin. When the script detects a valid wallet address, the script attempts to replace it with an attacker-controlled wallet address. Cookie theft and screen capture Cookie theft and screen capture happens only when a valid crypto wallet address is replaced and the element is visible. In that case, the JavaScript payload script loaded the legitimate html2canvas.min.js to capture a screenshot of the page, along with the page URL, cookies, original wallet address, and other metadata. This data is sent to the attacker endpoint https://1688360[.]cc/hit.php, likely so the operator can validate successful replacement activity and capture the victim’s session context. The JavaScript payload could collect browser cookies from the affected website, with some exceptions such as if the HttpOnly flag was set. This could cause users to unknowingly send cryptocurrency to the attacker instead of the intended recipient.Payment card skimmingLater versions of the payload added payment card skimming functionality. The script monitors input and textarea elements, keyboard events, form submissions, and web requests for payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV values on the compromised website. Captured card data was to an attacker-controlled endpoint (1688360[.]cc/card.php). Note the skimmer could not read payment details entered inside secure cross-origin payment iframes, such as hosted payment fields from providers like Stripe or Adyen.Attempted iOS exploit delivery For visitors using iPhones or iPads, the malware reportedly attempted to load the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits. The payload used device and browser checks to decide whether to attempt iOS-specific exploitation. When the payload identified a visitor’s device as an iPhone or iPad, it added two script elements to the page to load external JavaScript files. Indicators of these pages are the elements data-channel-code, data-chain-url, and data-cfasync attributes.The script injected a hidden iframe in some cases (hxxps://eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu/JIUJIU888/weifile[.]html) on devices it identified as running iOS 18.6 or earlier. The iframe is positioned off-screen with zero width and height, suggesting it is not intended to be visible to the user. iOS exploit delivery componentstrack.js is the browser-side payload. It checks for iOS or iPadOS and loads additional components when it detects either operating system.boot.js is the main iOS loader. It uses Safari and iOS version information to select the next delivery path.weifile.html provides a separate delivery path for selected iOS and iPadOS versions. It loads index.js.index.js initializes an obfuscated loader, decodes embedded modules, reports device and domain metadata, and may fetch additional modules (if required). The following table summarizes the two modules embedded in index.js.Embedded Module IdentifierDescription57620206d62079baad0e57e6d9ec93120c0f5247Utility/runtime helper module providing encoding, binary parsing, numeric conversion, URL normalization, and typed-array/DataView helpers.14669ca3b1519ba2a8f40be287f646d4d7593eb0Browser environment profiling and anti-analysis module that checks runtime capabilities, storage behavior, WebRTC, MathML rendering, WebAssembly behavior, and automation indicators such as navigator.webdriver.Table 1: Functions of the two modules embedded in index.js. ConclusionThe Optimizely incident highlights how attackers can compromise trusted third-party JavaScript supply chains to reach users across many websites at once. By abusing a legitimate experimentation feature, the attacker delivered injected JavaScript through snippets that affected websites already trusted. Note the malicious JavaScript code can run in visitors’ browsers without any obvious change to the page. The card-skimming and wallet-replacement behavior should be understood as page-context activity, not browser-wide monitoring. These scripts act within the compromised site where they are loaded. Broader impact would depend on successful exploitation by the iOS/WebKit exploit chain. Regional Insights: 2027 State of Threat Intelligence
items.summary: Recorded Future’s 2027 State of Threat Intelligence report surveyed 768 security professionals worldwide on how they use threat intelligence today, how they apply AI to it, and where they plan to invest. The report presents the global findings. The regional executive summaries in this blog cover insights from the same survey, breaking data down by global region into dedicated briefs covering the specific conclusions for cybersecurity leaders in North America , EMEA , APJ , and LATAM . Start with your region to see how your peers are approaching threat intelligence, and read the others for a wider view. North America (United States and Canada) In North America, threat intelligence now informs decisions well beyond the security organization. Five teams consume it on average, and 85% of organizations surveyed have teams outside core security using it , including risk management (54%), fraud prevention (44%), and risk and compliance (44%). With intelligence supporting this many teams, 81% plan to invest more in the next 12 months. The challenge is getting the right intelligence to each of those teams in a form they can act on. Doing that depends on how well intelligence comes together, and this is an ongoing effort for many programs. Most surveyed organizations (63%) draw on four or more intelligence vendors. Only 21% combine that external intelligence with their own internal telemetry in a single platform, where analysts can see which threats apply to their environment. Consolidation plans reflect this. Of the 76% planning to consolidate, the largest share are doing it to improve correlation across signals (40%), compared with only 8% who cite cost. Moving intelligence from those sources to risk owners is also largely manual. 54% put intelligence into action manually across tools and processes. Among organizations sharing intelligence outside security, 38% rely on ad hoc messages or scheduled reports. Manual handoffs make it harder to see what risk owners did with the intelligence and whether it worked. While 98% measure program value, 28% track whether triggered actions were effective. Only 22% report closed-loop operationalization, where stakeholders act on intelligence, the results are validated, and those results inform the program’s priorities and collection. AI is already part of this work for nearly all respondents ( 98% ), and 60% use agents that take actions inside their intelligence tools. Leaders become more cautious as the stakes rise: comfort with letting AI act falls from 71% for summarization to 56% for enforcement actions. The leading barriers are lack of auditability (40%) and unproven accuracy (31%). 73% say intelligence regularly feeds their AI and automation systems or is a core input to them. That makes the quality and correlation of their intelligence a factor in how far they can trust AI to act. Risk owners can come from procurement, legal, fraud, corporate security, or communications. Threat intelligence innovation means getting the intelligence to the right person to make decisions and take action based on that intelligence. Rich LaTulip North America Field CISO at Recorded Future This summary draws on responses from 347 North American security professionals . They were part of a global survey of 768 that asked how organizations use threat intelligence, apply AI to it, and plan future investments. The full report covers how intelligence is expanding across the business, what full visibility requires, and what stands between teams and proven impact.

items.title: Russian charged with spying on Palantir employees for Moscow
items.summary: Igor Andreevich D’iu, A Russian national recruited through Telegram, has been charged in the United States with acting as a Moscow agent in a surveillance campaign targeting employees of a defense technology company, understood to be Palantir Technologies.
